Author
Affiliation

1 Introduction

1.1 Motivation

In Electronic Design and Automation (EDA) for Integrated Circuits (ICs), a schematic presents an abstraction in comparison to the layout that will eventually be taped-out and fabricated by the semiconductor foundry.

While in the schematic, a connection between device terminals is seen as an equipotential, the stacked geometries in a specific layout introduce parasitic effects, which can be thought of additional resistors, capacitors (and inductors), not modeled by and missing in the original schematic.

To be able to simulate these effects, a parasitic extraction tool (PEX) is used, to extract a netlist from the layout, which represents the original schematic (created from the layout active and passive elements) augmented with the additional parasitic devices.

1.3 About KLayout-PEX

KLayout is an open source VLSI layout viewer and editor.

KLayout-PEX (short KPEX) is a PEX tool, well integrated with KLayout by using its API.

There are multiple PEX engines supported, currently:

  • FasterCap integration (field solver engine)
  • FastCap2 integration (field solver engine, selected with --fastcap)
  • MAGIC integration (wrapper calling magic)
  • Analytical 2.5D engine (parasitic concepts and formulas of MAGIC, implemented using KLayout methods)
Tip

KPEX tool source code itself is made publicly available on GitHub (follow this link) and shared under the GPL-3.0 license.

KPEX documentation source code is made publicly available on GitHub (follow this link) and shared under the Apache-2.0 license.

Please feel free to create issues and/or submit pull requests on GitHub to fix errors and omissions!

The production of the tool and this document would be impossible without these (and many more) great open-source software products: KLayout, FasterCap, FastCap2, MAGIC, Palace, Elmer, OpenRCX, KQCircuits, protobuf, Quarto, Python, ngspice, Numpy, Scipy, Matplotlib, Git, Docker, Ubuntu, Linux…

1.4 Status

Caution

Currently, KPEX is developed as a Python prototype, using the KLayout Python API. This allows for a faster development cycle during the current prototyping phase.

Eventually, critical parts will be re-implemented in Rust and parallelized to improve performance.

Warning

KPEX is experimental. Extraction and consistency checks do not establish calibrated accuracy for every device or layout.

RC includes coupling capacitances. There is no separate RCC value for --mode.

1.5 Installation

Generally, KPEX is deployed using PyPi (Python Package Index), install via:

pip3 install --upgrade klayout-pex

kpex --version   # check the installed version 
kpex --help      # this will help with command line arguments

As for the dependencies, there are multiple options available.

1.5.1 Option 1: Using IIC-OSIC-TOOLS Docker Image

We provide a comprehensive, low entry barrier Docker image that comes pre-installed with most relevant open source ASIC tools, as well as the open PDKs. This is a pre-compiled Docker image which allows to do circuit design on a virtual machine on virtually any type of computing equipment (personal PC, Raspberry Pi, cloud server) on various operating systems (Windows, macOS, Linux).

For further information please look at the Docker Hub page and for detailed instructions at the IIC-OSIC-TOOLS GitHub page.

WarningLinux

In this document, we assume that users have a basic knowledge of Linux and how to operate it using the terminal (shell). If you are not yet familiar with Linux (which is basically a must when doing integrated circuit design as many tools are only available on Linux), then please check out a Linux introductory course or tutorial online, there are many resources available.

A summary of important Linux shell commands is provided in IIC-JKU Linux Cheatsheet.

1.5.2 Option 2: Standalone Installation

  • KLayout layout tool:
    • is mandatory for all engines (besides the MAGIC-wrapper)
    • get the latest pre-built package version
    • or follow the build instructions
  • FasterCap engine:
    • optional, required to run the FasterCap engine
    • either compile your own version from the GitHub repository
    • or use precompiled versions available at https://github.com/iic-jku/FasterCap/releases
  • MAGIC-wrapper engine:
    • optional, required to run the MAGIC-wrapper engine
    • use MAGIC 8.3.693 or newer for the corrected sidewall counting (see Section 5.4)
    • Follow the installation instructions at the GitHub repository
  • Skywater sky130A PDK:
    • optional, for now, KPEX technology specific files are deployed within the klayout-pex Python package
    • pip3 install --upgrade ciel (install PDK package manager)
    • ciel ls-remote --pdk sky130A (retrieve available PDK releases
      • for example PRE-RELEASE 0c1df35fd535299ea1ef74d1e9e15dedaeb34c32 (2024.12.11))
    • ciel enable --pdk sky130A 0c1df35fd535299ea1ef74d1e9e15dedaeb34c32 (install a PDK version)
    • PDK files now have been installed under $HOME/.volare/sky130A
  • IHP SG13G2 PDK:
    • optional, for now, KPEX technology specific files are deployed within the klayout-pex Python package
    • pip3 install --upgrade ciel (install PDK package manager)
    • ciel ls-remote --pdk ihp-sg13g2 (retrieve available PDK releases
      • for example PRE-RELEASE cb7daaa8901016cf7c5d272dfa322c41f024931f (2025.07.18))
    • ciel enable --pdk ihp-sg13g2 cb7daaa8901016cf7c5d272dfa322c41f024931f (install a PDK version)
    • PDK files now have been installed under $HOME/.volare/ihp-sg13g2

1.5.3 Checking Tool Versions

The Python package requires klayout>=0.30.12. KLayout 0.30.13 is recommended for terminal-lookup performance, neighborhood-visitor memory fixes and resistance-extraction crash fixes. The recommendation is a warning, so an environment still shipping 0.30.12 can run.

The CLI checks the Python module and the executable separately when both are used. Updating one does not update the other. An LVS-database-only extraction can use the module without the executable. The runtime table lists the version found, the required range and the recommended range.

An unrecognized tool version is reported as unchecked. warn and off do not repair the numerical or performance defects of an older executable.

For --magic, KPEX 0.9.0 requires MAGIC 8.3.693 or newer, which removes an extra sidewall halving. Pure --2.5D extraction does not require a MAGIC executable. The remaining multi-polygon device-terminal limitation is separate from the recommendation to upgrade KLayout and is not resolved by installing 0.30.13.

1.5.4 Useful tools: meshlab

For previewing generated 3D geometries, representing the input to FasterCap, we recommend installing MeshLab. The generated STL-files are located at output/<design>/Geometries/*.stl.

2 First Steps

  • The command line tool kpex is used to trigger the parasitic extraction flow from the terminal.
  • Get extraction help with kpex extract --help
  • Inspect or reduce netlists with the separate netlist command
  • Inspect interchange files with the separate pex25d command

2.1 Example Layouts

Example layouts are included in the testdata/designs subdirectory of the KLayout-PEX source code:

git clone https://github.com/iic-jku/klayout-pex.git
cd klayout-pex

# for sky130A
find testdata/designs/sky130A -name "*.gds.gz"

# for IHP SG13G2
find testdata/designs/ihp-sg13g2 -name "*.gds.gz"

2.2 Running KPEX/2.5D

From the KPEX source directory:

kpex extract --pdk sky130A --2.5D --mode RC --blackbox y \
  --gds testdata/designs/sky130A/test_patterns/nfet_li1.gds.gz \
  --out-netlist nfet_li1-rc.spice

CC extracts capacitances with one equipotential node per net. R resolves the wire resistance, and RC adds the coupling capacitances to that distributed network. --blackbox y retains recognized device models instead of extracting their modeled capacitor interiors. Select it explicitly because the current prototype defaults to whiteboxing for development.

Use --schematic to follow an existing testbench interface (Section 6.4). RC enables consistency failures by default; Section 8 explains the diagnostics and the additional checks that can be requested.

Grounded capacitance is an explicit approximation: --mode C uses ideal conductors, while --mode RC --coupling grounded retains distributed resistance. The development-version options, floating-conductor treatment and standalone postprocessing are described in Section 7.

Each run directory contains kpex_result.json, which records the output paths, warnings, errors and final status. A written netlist can coexist with failed checks, so inspect the exit status and diagnostics before simulation.

2.3 Generating PEX25D

kpex pex25d generates a PEX25D geometry and material description without running a solver. It is separate from the analytical KPEX/2.5D engine. See Section 11.1 for the format specification, benefits, and standalone tools.

From the KLayout-PEX source directory:

kpex pex25d --pdk sky130A --blackbox y \
  --gds testdata/designs/sky130A/nmos_diode2/nmos_diode2.gds.gz \
  --out-file nmos_diode2.pex25d \
  --out-scene nmos_diode2.pex25d.scene.pb

The .pex25d file contains the text representation. The .pex25d.scene.pb file contains the resolved protobuf scene, including absolute layer heights and terminal intersections. Generation runs the reference validator by default; diagnostics determine the exit code even when output files have been written.

Use the standalone tool to inspect or validate an artifact:

pex25d show nmos_diode2.pex25d
pex25d validate nmos_diode2.pex25d --strict

For a complete, hand-written file that can be validated and exported without layout generation, use the downloadable example in Section 11.1.4. Terminal semantics and the current state of KLayout-generated terminals are explained in Section 11.1.5.9. For explicit capacitance result exclusions that retain physical geometry and shielding, use the downloadable accounting variant in Section 11.1.5.7.2.

2.4 Running the KPEX/FasterCap engine

Preconditions:

  • klayout-pex was installed, see Section 1.5
  • FasterCap was installed, see Section 1.5
Note

Normally, devices with SPICE (Nagel 1975) simulation models (e.g. like MOM-capacitors1 in the sky130A PDK) are ignored (“blackboxed”) during parasitic extraction.

kpex has an option --blackbox n to allow extraction of those devices (whiteboxing), which can be useful during development (during the prototype phase, whiteboxing is actually the default setting, so please use --blackbox y to explicitly configure blackboxing).

Let’s try the following:

kpex extract --pdk sky130A --blackbox n --gds \
  testdata/designs/sky130A/*/cap_vpp_04p4x04p6_l1m1m2_noshield.gds.gz
Note

This will report an error that we have not activated one or more engines, and list the available engines:

Argument Description
--fastercap Run kpex/FasterCap engine
--2.5D Run kpex/2.5D engine
--magic Run MAGIC engine

Now, to run the FasterCap engine (might take a couple of minutes):

kpex extract --pdk sky130A --blackbox n --fastercap --gds \
  testdata/designs/sky130A/*/cap_vpp_04p4x04p6_l1m1m2_noshield.gds.gz

Within the output directory (defaults to output), KPEX creates a subdirectory Geometries, containing STL-files that provide a preview of the FasterCap input geometries. Use MeshLab (see Section 1.5.4) to open and preview those files:

ls -d output/cap_vpp_04*/Geometries/*.stl
Tip
  • Open the *.stl files in MeshLab
  • Use the eye buttons to hide and show each file/mesh
  • Use the align tool (“A” in the toolbar) to assign different colors
  • Start by showing only on the conductors (files named cond_*.stl)
  • Then try showing different dielectrics (files named diel_*.stl), to see how they surround the conductors.

In the log file, we see the output of FasterCap including the Maxwell capacitance matrix:

Capacitance matrix is:
Dimension 3 x 3
g1_VSUBS  5.2959e-09 -4.46971e-10 -1.67304e-09
g2_C1  -5.56106e-10 1.5383e-08 -1.47213e-08
g3_C0  -1.69838e-09 -1.48846e-08 1.64502e-08

KPEX interprets this matrix and prints a CSV netlist, which can be pasted into a spreadsheet application:

Device;Net1;Net2;Capacitance [fF]
Cext_0_1;VSUBS;C1;0.5
Cext_0_2;VSUBS;C0;1.69
Cext_1_2;C1;C0;14.8
Cext_1_1;C1;VSUBS;0.08

In addition, a SPICE netlist is generated.

2.5 Running the KPEX/MAGIC engine

Preconditions:

  • klayout-pex was installed, see Section 1.5
  • magic was installed, see Section 1.5

The MAGIC section of kpex extract --help describes the arguments and their defaults. Important arguments:

  • --magicrc: specify location of the magicrc file
  • --gds: path to the GDS input layout
  • --magic: enable magic engine
kpex extract --pdk sky130A --magic --gds \
  testdata/designs/sky130A/*/cap_vpp_04p4x04p6_l1m1m2_noshield.gds.gz

3 Choosing and describing PDKs

A PDK2 supplies more than a list of GDS layer numbers. KPEX needs to know which shapes conduct, how they connect, what surrounds them in three dimensions, and which part of a device is already represented by its circuit model. The technology definition keeps these choices together, while the extraction algorithms remain independent of the PDK.

3.1 Choosing the process variant

--pdk selects a complete combination of extraction deck, layer stack, parasitic tables and device mappings. Choose the variant used by the layout and its simulation models. Changing only a top-metal name cannot turn one stack into another.

The older spelling ihp_sg13g2 remains an alias for ihp-sg13g2. Use the hyphenated spelling in new commands and scripts. The other three spellings in Table 3 are the accepted identifiers, including their capitalization.

This is a list of extraction configurations, not a claim that every device of each PDK has a simulation mapping. An extracted device without a supported mapping produces an error instead of a guessed model call.

3.2 Forming nets and identifying layers

The PEX extraction decks use KLayout’s LVS facilities to recognize devices and establish connectivity. This step produces the flat netlist and the named, net-associated polygons in the LVSDB. Comparing that result with a schematic is a separate operation.

The deck and technology definition must agree on the meaning of each computed layer. A name alone is insufficient: a piece of drawn metal may have a different role inside a capacitor than outside it.

There are three identities to keep distinct:

  • The computed layer identifies polygons produced by the extraction deck, including their net and device role
  • The original layer selects the physical layer’s parasitic coefficients
  • The process layer selects its position and material environment in the three-dimensional stack

For example, the ihp-sg13g2 deck splits drawn Metal5 into ordinary routing, MIM3 bottom-plate and device-related regions. All use coefficients keyed by Metal5, but their process layers distinguish metal under the MIM dielectric from ordinary metal.

The computed-layer kind also specifies whether a region is ordinary conductor, a modeled capacitor plate, a resistor region, or device-internal geometry. This is why removing a capacitor from the parasitic sum does not necessarily remove its plates from shielding or from coupling to other nets. See Section 6 and the section on excluding parts of the layout for the extraction choices.

When adding a deck, assign stable names with name(layer, name). Keep the named device regions and the technology’s layer identities consistent. A pin label, a device plate and a physical routing layer are different contracts even when they originate from the same drawn GDS layer.

3.3 Keeping technology data together

The technology definition uses a Protocol Buffers schema and is distributed as JSON. Its parts answer different questions:

The main schema is tech.proto. It incorporates process_stack.proto, process_parasitics.proto, device_models.proto and the substrate definition. These schemas define the data contract; the generated JSON contains the values for a particular variant.

Changing a dielectric height does not automatically refit the KPEX/2.5D coefficients. The stack and tables are separate inputs. This matters when comparing a three-dimensional solve with the table-based engine: both must describe the same intended physical process.

3.4 Describing the process stack

For 3D solvers, like the KPEX/FasterCap engine, 3D information about the dimensions (e.g. z-offset and thickness) of metal layers is required, as well as the dielectrics in-between.

The sky130A stack illustrates why a list of metal heights alone is not enough: several different dielectric profiles surround the same conductor.

The stack distinguishes conductors from the material around them:

  • Metals such as poly, metal1 and metal5 have a thickness and a bottom height relative to the substrate
  • Contacts and vias, such as licon and via1, connect conductors on adjacent levels
  • Sidewall dielectrics, such as IOX and SPNIT, use conformal profiles with lateral thickness and no thickness in the field. A profile may also cover the metal top
  • Conformal dielectrics, such as LINT and TOPNIT, specify thickness above metal, beside it and in the field
  • Simple dielectrics, such as PSG and NILD2, fill the remaining region between levels

Physical corners can change these profiles and manufactured widths. Section 3.9.11.1 describes the available source recipes, and Section 3.9.11.6 distinguishes incremental coating offsets from cumulative field extents.

The relative permittivity \(k\) belongs to each dielectric. A stack may therefore contain several dielectric boundaries around one piece of metal. The schematic labels above and the technology’s physical-layer names need not be identical; their correspondence is explicit in the technology definition.

The schema excerpt below shows how these relationships are expressed:

  • ProcessStackInfo.layers orders the layers of the stack
  • LayerInfo.layer_type identifies the layer kind with a LayerType enum value
  • Its parameters payload must match that kind
  • MetalLayer.z locates the metal bottom relative to the substrate
  • MetalLayer.contact_above describes the contact to the next conductor
  • MetalLayer.line_width_bias changes total manufactured width for physical export
  • MetalLayer.physical_geometry_unavailable marks a profile whose physical law is unqualified
  • A dielectric reference identifies the layer or profile it wraps
  • Wrapping can be nested: SPNIT wraps IOX, which wraps poly
message ProcessStackInfo {

    enum LayerType { …
        LAYER_TYPE_SIMPLE_DIELECTRIC = 50;
        LAYER_TYPE_CONFORMAL_DIELECTRIC = 60;
        LAYER_TYPE_METAL = 80;
    }

    message Contact { // Contact/Via
        string name = 1;
        string layer_below = 9;
        string metal_above = 10;
        double thickness = 20;

        double width = 30;
        double spacing = 31;
        double border = 32;
    } 
    …
    message SimpleDielectricLayer { // Simple dielectric
        double dielectric_k = 10;
        string reference = 30;
    }

    message ConformalDielectricLayer { // Conformal dielectric
        double dielectric_k = 10;
        double thickness_over_metal = 20;
        double thickness_where_no_metal = 21;
        double thickness_sidewall = 22;
        string reference = 30;
    }

    message MetalLayer { // Metal
        // Bottom height above substrate and thickness, in µm
        double z = 1;
        double thickness = 2;
        double line_width_bias = 20;
        bool physical_geometry_unavailable = 30;
        Contact contact_above = 40;
    }

    message LayerInfo {
        string name = 1;
        LayerType layer_type = 2;
        oneof parameters { …
            SimpleDielectricLayer simple_dielectric_layer = 50;
            ConformalDielectricLayer conformal_dielectric_layer = 60;
            MetalLayer metal_layer = 70;
        }
    }

    repeated LayerInfo layers = 100;
}

3.4.1 Planar passivation over gf180mcuD

The top surface is an instructive example of why the reference of a dielectric matters. For the selected 1P5M/11KA/MIM-B stack, the maintained cross-section drawing gives the oxide surface relative to the bottom of Metal5.

Metal5 is \(1.1925\,\mu\mathrm{m}\) thick. The planar oxide surface is \(2.3925\,\mu\mathrm{m}\) above its bottom, leaving \(1.2\,\mu\mathrm{m}\) of oxide over the metal. A \(0.3\,\mu\mathrm{m}\) nitride layer sits above that surface. Its relative permittivity is \(7\), while the oxide uses \(4\), as recorded in the maintained dielectric table.

The technology expresses these planar surfaces using two wrapped dielectric profiles:

  • pass wraps Metal5, with \(1.2\,\mu\mathrm{m}\) above metal and \(2.3925\,\mu\mathrm{m}\) in the field
  • sin wraps pass, with \(0.3\,\mu\mathrm{m}\) above the oxide and \(2.6925\,\mu\mathrm{m}\) in the field
  • Both use zero sidewall growth, preserving flat interfaces over the gap

The field height of sin includes the oxide height because it is measured from the root metal’s bottom. Treating it as only \(0.3\,\mu\mathrm{m}\) would place nitride near the bottom of the gap instead of above the oxide.

The general dielectric table lists \(2.3\,\mu\mathrm{m}\) for the 11KA oxide. KPEX uses the detailed cross-section’s \(2.3925\,\mu\mathrm{m}\) consistently with the metal thickness from the same drawing. This is an explicit source choice, not a fitted capacitance correction. The maintained community PDK repository is the source of these dimensions.

3.5 Interpreting parasitic coefficients

The capacitance tables are a compact model of geometry. Each family has different dimensions because it multiplies a different geometric quantity. Mixing their units can yield plausible-looking values with the wrong scale.

For an overlap area \(A\) and area coefficient \(c_A\), the model contribution is \(C=c_A A\). The coefficient is per square micrometre. A perimeter or fringe coefficient instead multiplies a length, and the fringe calculation supplies the fraction left after distance limits and shielding.

The sidewall coefficient has a different form. For two facing parallel edges of length \(L\), gap \(s\) and fitted offset \(o\), the table convention is

\[ C_{\mathrm{pair}}=b\,\frac{L}{s_{\mathrm{eff}}}, \qquad s_{\mathrm{eff}}=\max(s+o,s/2). \]

The ratio of lengths is dimensionless, so \(b\) is in attofarads. It is not an area density or a capacitance per micrometre. A negative fitted offset is allowed; the lower bound on effective separation prevents a zero or negative denominator for positive gaps. For a varying gap, integrate this density along the edge instead of substituting an average gap.

This equation defines the full-pair coefficient convention. In KPEX 0.9.0, each of the two directed visits contributes half, so their sum follows this law. Earlier versions applied an extra halving. The coefficient must not be doubled to compensate for that older behavior: contribution counting and physical table values are separate parts of the model.

The stored capacitance units are attofarads; extraction reports commonly use femtofarads, with \(1000\,\mathrm{aF}=1\,\mathrm{fF}\). Resistance tables use milliohms per square for sheets and milliohms per contact or via cut.

3.5.1 Direction and physical consistency

A side-overlap row from an edge on Metal1 toward a conductor on Metal2 describes a different geometric contribution from a row in the reverse direction. These coefficients can differ without violating reciprocal capacitance: the final coupling of a node pair includes the applicable contributions, not a choice of just one directional row.

Physical comparisons need the whole environment:

  • Equal conductor spacing and equal dielectric material give the same parallel-plate density
  • Equal gaps alone do not imply equal sidewall fits when height above substrate or nearby conductors differs
  • Variants with identical complete conductor and dielectric surroundings should not acquire different values solely from renaming layers
  • A changed fit can alter both \(b\) and \(o\), so compare its predicted capacitance over the relevant gaps

Shared lower-layer dimensions do not make two complete stacks identical. Different upper metals or passivation can change the fitted capacitance of those lower conductors.

The tables are based in part on the extraction sections of MAGIC technology files. Importing those values does not import MAGIC’s layer classification, device recognition, shielding or grid rounding. Agreement of one test pattern therefore does not establish agreement for every layout.

3.6 Mapping extracted devices to circuit models

An LVS device class is not necessarily the model name or primitive type expected by a simulator. The mapping declares:

  • The instance prefix, such as M or X
  • The target model or subcircuit name
  • The order of its terminals
  • Which parameters are exported, their names and their conversion factors
  • Fixed parameters, such as an RF-mode selector

For example, the ihp-sg13* LVS class rfnmos maps to an X call of sg13_lv_nmos with rfmode=1. Its terminal order is D, G, S, B. The mapping supplies this information explicitly instead of assuming that every four-terminal device is a native MOS model.

Lengths and areas also need an explicit contract. An ihp-sg13* LVS length stored in micrometres is exported to the model in metres using lvs_parameter_factor=1e-6. An area needs the square of that length factor. A mapping may give schematic_parameter_factors for different SPICE prefixes: a native M device read with geometry scaling and an X wrapper parameter do not have identical unit semantics. These factors describe the PDK model interface; they are separate from the netlist’s .option scale setting.

For symmetric area/perimeter models, the mapping can recover equivalent rectangle sides from area \(A\) and perimeter \(P\). The sides solve \(wl=A\) and \(2(w+l)=P\). This preserves those two geometric quantities without claiming to recover the original orientation. It is unsuitable for a transistor or varactor whose model depends differently on width and length.

3.6.1 Independent capacitance references

A KIND_METAL_CAPACITOR mapping can also contain capacitance_references. These describe the nominal mutual capacitance of a particular unordered terminal pair. They are used by the device-capacitance check, not to tune the extraction result.

Each reference states:

  • Two terminal names whose local plates can be compared
  • A capacitance expression in farads, using mapped model parameters
  • Optional derived parameters and a validity condition
  • A source and its nominal assumptions

The instance multiplier belongs in the reference exactly once. A validity condition restricts the expression to the supported geometry; it is not permission to extrapolate outside the model’s domain. The check evaluates the recorded expression without running a simulator or searching arbitrary SPICE libraries.

The bundled references currently cover cap_cmomf and cap_cmomi in ihp-sg13*. The cap_cmomf reference uses nominal area density and the selected metal count. The cap_cmomi reference additionally reflects its discrete finger array and feed option. Their provenance is pinned to the device model sources.

These references do not include process-corner or mismatch variation. Some densities are estimates or derived from a sibling stack, as stated in each reference’s description. A ratio between extracted and nominal capacitance helps find a discrepancy; it does not by itself identify which model is physically correct. Unlisted device pairs have no such reference check.

3.7 Updating technology data

The built-in definitions are produced by Python generators4. The generated JSON and Python schema modules are packaged in the distribution, but are not committed source files in the code repository. Editing an installed JSON file is temporary: a rebuild or package upgrade replaces it.

For a source change:

  1. Change the relevant PDK generator and maintain its source records, assumptions and data-revision history as in Section 3.9.5
  2. Run ./gen_tech_pb.sh from the klayout-pex checkout to regenerate the schema modules and all built-in JSON definitions
  3. Compare the resulting tables by physical layer and coefficient family
  4. Check the affected geometries and sibling variants before interpreting changed extraction values

The generators contain deliberate projections, not only verbatim copies of upstream tables. Diffusion rows may be shared between extracted implant or tap regions. MIM plates retain their model-derived plate coupling while surrounding parasitics come from other rows. Resistance overrides have their own sources. A table refresh must preserve these distinctions and show changed values for review.

The nominal sky130A and gf180mcuD tables in KPEX 0.9.0 follow the maintained open-pdks extraction sources. The ihp-sg13g2 and ihp-sg13cmos5l tables use the corrected extraction fits at 14b1ab8. These refreshes preserve the diffusion and MIM derivations and resistance overrides. They do not change the independent device-model references. Automatic calibration and selectable capacitance corners are not available in 0.9.0. The development version adds complete low/high capacitance components for all four PDKs; Section 3.9.7 explains their selection and the remaining qualification limits. Both IHP variants also provide isolated GatPoly sheet-resistance sensitivities, described in Section 3.9.8.

The sky130A development catalog also provides four fixed-layout resistance sensitivities with explicit MIM sheet bounds. Their source-dependent overrides, engineering assumptions and via-stack example are described in Section 3.9.10.

3.8 Inspecting the generated definitions

The previews below show the complete resolved nominal Technology messages for the development version following 0.9.0. They contain the selected coefficients, physical stack and device interfaces used by extraction. The catalog examples in Section 3.9.3 show how these components are selected and how their provenance is recorded.

To inspect the data actually installed, locate klayout_pex_protobuf beside the klayout_pex package in site-packages5. The resolved nominal snapshots use the PDK identifiers from Table 3, followed by _tech.pb.json. The catalogs and their component datasets are under tech/<PDK>/.

Each process-stack layer declares its kind in layer_type and supplies exactly one matching parameters payload. For example, LAYER_TYPE_METAL requires metal_layer. Unspecified or unknown kinds, missing payloads and mismatches are rejected when the technology is loaded.

  • sky130A
  • gf180mcuD
  • ihp-sg13g2
  • ihp-sg13cmos5l
















































3.9 Selecting Technology Corners


An extraction corner selects the data used to calculate parasitics. It does not automatically select transistor models, temperature or supply voltage for the subsequent simulation. Those choices can be independent in an open PDK.












Note







Corner selection belongs to the development version following 0.9.0. Each supported technology supplies complete nominal, low and high capacitance components. A custom scenario can select those components explicitly.


The development catalogs also provide:


    

  • Isolated IHP GatPoly sheet-resistance sensitivities (Section 3.9.8)
    • 

  • Complete ihp-sg13cmos5l fixed-layout resistance sensitivities (Section 3.9.9)
    • 

  • sky130A resistance sensitivities with explicit MIM sheet bounds (Section 3.9.10)
    • 

  • Independent MIM device-reference components (Section 3.9.12)
    • 

  • Source-related physical recipes (Section 3.9.11.1)
    • 



These selections retain their documented assumptions. An upstream style name does not automatically declare a matching physical stack or a correlated process corner.








3.9.1 Selecting Declared Scenarios


Both kpex extract and kpex pex25d accept --corner. A scenario names complete resistance, capacitance, physical-stack and optional device-reference datasets. With no explicit option, the catalog’s declared default is selected.


kpex extract --pdk sky130A --2.5D --mode RC --corner nominal \
  --gds r_wire_voltage_divider_li1.gds.gz \
  --out-netlist divider.spice --out-result divider-result.json


GDS: https://github.com/iic-jku/klayout-pex/blob/main/testdata/designs/sky130A/test_patterns/r_wire_voltage_divider_li1.gds.gz


This example uses the bundled nominal data and a distributed wire pattern. Omitting --corner nominal produces the same technology selection while nominal is the catalog default.


A separately supplied catalog can be selected explicitly:


kpex extract --pdk sky130A --2.5D --mode RC \
  --tech-catalog path/to/catalog.pb.json --corner nominal \
  --gds r_wire_voltage_divider_li1.gds.gz \
  --out-netlist divider.spice


The catalog must identify the selected --pdk. A catalog for one process cannot silently change the layout/LVS interface of another. Scenario identifiers are case-sensitive: nominal and Nominal are different names.


Unknown selections fail before the layout or LVS database is read. The diagnostic lists the valid scenarios, so a typo cannot silently fall back to nominal extraction.








3.9.2 Keeping the Sources Independent


The four datasets answer different physical questions:







Layout layers, computed-layer identities, device interfaces, substrate connectivity and exclusion definitions remain shared. Selection resolves a fresh complete technology before extraction caches are constructed. Running one corner and then another does not accumulate table rows or modify a previous selection.















A missing table entry is not the same as an explicit zero. Each selected resistance and capacitance table must cover the same row keys as the default scenario. Complete components can be shared by several scenarios without inheriting unspecified numerical entries from nominal data.








3.9.3 Inspecting Catalog Data


The following examples contain the generated pb.json files for the current corner implementation. Each complete example includes its catalog, shared technology, all four nominal datasets, and both additional capacitance datasets (low and high). The bundles also contain the available resistance, MIM device-reference and physical-stack components described below. Unpack a bundle before passing its catalog to --tech-catalog; component paths are relative to that catalog.







For example, the sky130A catalog selects separate resistance, capacitance, physical-stack and device-reference datasets. The shared technology supplies the layer and device interfaces.


The catalog and datasets each have a description. A TechnologyFile reference identifies the file by path and sha256; the description and provenance belong to the referenced content.




  • sky130A catalog
  • gf180mcuD catalog
  • ihp-sg13g2 catalog
  • ihp-sg13cmos5l catalog
























































3.9.4 Tracing Sources and Assumptions


Each catalog and dataset has structured provenance:







A source must identify a revision or an exact SHA256 digest. Extraction records these references without downloading them. A source revision identifies the input document, while data_revision identifies the KPEX interpretation of that input. The two can change independently.


For example, the ihp-sg13g2 capacitance dataset identifies the corrected extraction file at 14b1ab8. Its resistance dataset separately records the nominal GatPoly and MIM assumptions. The device-reference dataset cites its independent MOM models. A common process name does not make those sources interchangeable.


An assumption states both what was assumed and why. Diffusion projection and the thin-plate approximation for surrounding MIM coupling therefore remain visible alongside the imported coefficients. Recording an assumption does not establish a measured error bound or qualify a physical corner.








3.9.5 Maintaining Data History


Maintain history when reviewing a data change:


    

  1. Add new source records for changed upstream inputs, with new identifiers and pinned revisions or hashes
    2. 

  2. Describe changed assumptions and their physical reasons
    3. 

  3. Append a history entry with the change date, summary, reason and supporting source or review references
    4. 

  4. Set data_revision to that final entry’s revision, then regenerate the files and their catalog hashes
    5. 

  5. Compare the numerical tables and check the affected geometries and sibling variants
    6. 



Keep previous history entries and the source identities they reference unchanged. Entries are ordered from oldest to newest. Multiple revisions on one date are allowed. A build does not invent a new revision or timestamp, and revision labels are not interpreted as corner names or version ranges.


The catalog’s history describes its available components and declared scenarios. Each component retains its own history, so updating capacitance does not invent a resistance or physical-stack revision.


schema_version describes the catalog format. data_revision describes the data and its interpretation. File hashes identify exact serialized bytes, while the resolved payload hashes identify numerical inputs. A clarification of an assumption changes file identity without changing coefficient identity.


The technology format is under development before 1.0.0. After a schema change, regenerate the examples with the matching KPEX version. Assigned field numbers and JSON names will become compatibility contracts when the format is stabilized.








3.9.6 Reading Upstream Corner Names


The maintained MAGIC extraction decks for the supported technologies declare these R/C combinations:







The sources are the maintained OpenPDKs sky130 deck, OpenPDKs gf180mcu deck, and the corrected ihp-sg13g2 and ihp-sg13cmos5l decks.


These names do not define all nine products of low, nominal and high R/C. Nor do transistor labels such as tt, ff and ss imply an extraction corner. For example, the sky130 simulation library separates MOS corner selection from its R/C model sections.


KPEX also contains derived MIM and diffusion rows and resistance values from other process sources. An imported corner must resolve those rows explicitly. The presence of a high-C block in an extraction deck is not evidence for an otherwise undocumented MIM sheet-resistance limit.


Separate component files do not imply statistical independence of R and C. In sky130A, some resistance-model overrides differ between hrhc and hrlc, even though both names start with high R. Such sources require scenario-specific R datasets rather than one generic high-R component.








3.9.7 Using Low/High Capacitance Components


Each supported PDK has complete nominal, low and high capacitance datasets. The additional components cover substrate area and perimeter, overlap, fitted sidewall and directed fringe terms. They retain the diffusion projections and MIM construction used by the nominal technology, with the selected capacitance data.







Each catalog also declares capiche-low-c and capiche-high-c, selecting the source-related physical recipes described in Section 3.9.11.1.


The low tables agree between the reviewed hrlc and lrlc styles, and the high tables agree between hrhc and lrhc, for all four PDKs. This permits sharing each capacitance component across those resistance choices; it does not prove that resistance can be factored in the same way.


These are complete tables, not a global scale factor applied to nominal capacitance. A sidewall fit changes its numerator and spacing offset together, so a larger numerator alone does not identify the larger predicted capacitance. Compare the resulting law over the relevant geometry, as described in Section 3.5.


The component provenance records the source choices that complete the tables:


    

  • gf180mcuD: the missing low-C Metal2-to-well fringe row uses the same-corner substrate perimeter coefficient, with the established well-plane projection
    • 

  • ihp-sg13g2: the MIM area law varies with the selected data, while its literal edge coefficient remains unchanged, with the separate cap_cpara factor excluded from that edge law
    • 

  • Every PDK retains its explicit diffusion and surrounding-MIM coupling assumptions, without claiming matching physical-stack or device-reference data
    • 







3.9.7.1 Holding Resistance Nominal


A sensitivity study can deliberately hold resistance nominal and vary only capacitance. This is a user-defined comparison, not a claim that the foundry specifies that R/C combination as a correlated process corner.


The complete sky130A sensitivity example contains the same component bytes as the bundled catalog, plus two declared scenarios, nominal-r-low-c and nominal-r-high-c. Unpacking it creates the sky130A-sensitivity directory. Its default remains nominal, and the custom scenario definitions are recorded in a new catalog-history entry.


The low-C scenario selects:


{
  "id": "nominal-r-low-c",
  "resistance": "nominal",
  "capacitance": "low",
  "process_stack": "nominal",
  "physical_stack_matches": false,
  "device_references": ""
}


The high-C scenario selects "capacitance": "high" under its distinct scenario identifier. Both use the nominal stack only for compatible layer identities and conductor ordering. The physical_stack_matches: false and empty device_references declarations prevent that structural use from claiming matched solver geometry or independent corner-specific device references.








3.9.7.2 Comparing Extracted Couplings


The following commands use the same sky130A layout of overlapping li1 and met1 plates for all three selections. The CC mode retains mutual and substrate capacitances; the nominal resistance selection is present in the catalog but does not add resistors in this mode.


GDS: https://github.com/iic-jku/klayout-pex/blob/main/testdata/designs/sky130A/test_patterns/overlap_plates_100um_x_100um_li1_m1.gds.gz


unzip sky130A-sensitivity.zip
for corner in nominal nominal-r-low-c nominal-r-high-c; do
  kpex extract --pdk sky130A --2.5D --mode CC \
    --tech-catalog sky130A-sensitivity/catalog.pb.json \
    --corner "$corner" \
    --gds overlap_plates_100um_x_100um_li1_m1.gds.gz \
    --out-dir "output/$corner" \
    --out-netlist "output/$corner.spice" \
    --out-result "output/$corner.json"
done















The three extracted couplings in Figure 5 are:







\(C_{\mathrm{LU}}\) connects LOWER ↔︎ UPPER, \(C_{\mathrm{LS}}\) connects LOWER ↔︎ sky130_gnd, and \(C_{\mathrm{US}}\) connects UPPER ↔︎ sky130_gnd. These are individual netlist capacitors, not diagonal entries of a capacitance matrix. Each result JSON records the selected component identities and provenance.


The different ratios between the columns show why one multiplier cannot reproduce these tables. To study a distributed RC layout, use --mode RC with the same explicitly declared scenarios; resistance then remains nominal while capacitance varies.










3.9.8 Varying GatPoly Sheet Resistance


Both ihp-sg13g2 and ihp-sg13cmos5l provide gatpoly-low-sheet and gatpoly-high-sheet. They vary only the sheet resistance of extracted GatPoly interconnect. Every other layer, contact and via resistance, and all capacitance coefficients, remain explicitly nominal.


The values come directly from each process’s maintained interconnect tables: 6.2, 7.0 and 7.8 \(\Omega/\square\). The sources and hashes are recorded separately in the ihp-sg13g2 low-sheet dataset and the ihp-sg13cmos5l low-sheet dataset.


These are fixed-layout sensitivity selections. They do not apply the thickness or linewidth variation of a full process corner, select a transistor corner, or change temperature. Their nominal stack provides layer identities and ordering; physical_stack_matches: false prevents treating it as matched field-solver geometry. These sheet-only scenarios select no device-reference component. An automatic device-capacitance comparison requires a separately justified explicit reference.




3.9.8.1 Comparing Strip Resistance


The example LVS database contains one 10 µm × 0.5 µm GatPoly strip. Ports A and B span opposite ends, with no contacts and no recognized resistor device. The same conductor and pin definitions apply to both IHP variants.


for corner in nominal gatpoly-low-sheet gatpoly-high-sheet; do
  kpex extract --pdk ihp-sg13g2 --2.5D --mode R \
    --corner "$corner" --lvsdb ihp-gatpoly-strip.lvsdb \
    --out-dir "output/$corner" \
    --out-netlist "output/$corner.spice"
done


For this rectangle, the independent reference is


\[
R_{AB}=R_{\square}\frac{L}{W} = 20R_{\square}.
\]




















Repeating the commands with --pdk ihp-sg13cmos5l gives the same values. Circuit simulations in ngspice, Xyce and VACASK agree with the sheet law, including strips at the published 0.13 µm interconnect width and the next layout-grid step.






3.9.8.2 Keeping Compact Resistors Separate


A recognized rsil, rppd or rhigh resistor keeps its compact model, terminals and dimensions. Its modeled body is excluded from extracted interconnect. The rsil model has its own sheet parameters, effective-width correction and contact terms; applying those again to every drawn GatPoly polygon would mix two different resistance models.


For this reason, the selectable wire limits are 6.2 and 7.8 \(\Omega/\square\) from the interconnect tables, rather than the compact model’s 6.02 and 7.98 \(\Omega/\square\). No compact-model width shift is applied to the strip. Selecting one of these sensitivities does not select a compact-resistor simulation corner.










3.9.9 Varying CMOS5L Resistance at Fixed Geometry


The ihp-sg13cmos5l catalog provides fixed-layout-low-r and fixed-layout-high-r. They select complete resistance tables for the existing extracted interconnect layers, contacts and vias, while retaining nominal capacitance and the drawn geometry. Select a scenario with the usual extraction options:


kpex extract --pdk ihp-sg13cmos5l --2.5D --mode RC \
  --corner fixed-layout-low-r --gds design.gds \
  --out-netlist design-low-r.spice --out-result design-low-r.json


Use fixed-layout-high-r for the corresponding high-resistance extraction, or nominal for the unchanged default. The narrower gatpoly-low-sheet and gatpoly-high-sheet scenarios vary only GatPoly; all their other resistance rows remain nominal.




3.9.9.1 Applying Sheet and Contact Laws


A rectangular wire follows \(R=R_{\square}L/W\). Each layer has its own sheet resistance; the low/high scenarios therefore do not multiply the entire network by one common factor.







A contact or via contributes its per-cut resistance. With equipotential terminals on both sides, \(N\) identical cuts in parallel give \(R=R_{\mathrm{cut}}/N\). A real contact array also has access and spreading resistance in its conductors, which the resistance extraction retains.







These rows come from the variant’s maintained minimum, typical and maximum interconnect tables. In particular, those sources place TopVia1 between Metal4 and TopMetal1 and specify its \(0.42\,\mu\mathrm{m}\) square cut directly. This resolves the row left unspecified in the variant’s process-specification contact table.






3.9.9.2 Interpreting Resistance Sensitivity


The selection changes the interconnect material laws applied to the existing polygons. Compact-device models retain their own internal resistances and geometry rules. Diffusion regions remain ideal device-terminal endpoints under the existing extraction boundary.


The source interconnect files also vary physical parameters, including GatPoly thickness. The fixed-layout resistance selections do not apply those geometry changes, temperature variation or compact-model width corrections. They use nominal analytical capacitance and declare no matching field-solver stack or automatic device-capacitance references, as explained in Section 3.9.11.


The low-R dataset and high-R dataset record the exact source revisions, hashes and assumptions. Their source-defined resistance bounds are suitable for sensitivity studies; combining them with nonnominal capacitance requires an explicit scenario and a justified interpretation of that combination.








3.9.10 Varying sky130A Resistance


The sky130A catalog provides four fixed-layout resistance sensitivities. Each selects a complete resistance table and the corresponding low or high capacitance table. nominal remains the default.







The four resistance datasets retain differences that one generic high-R and one generic low-R table would lose. The source parameters rnw, rcvia3 and rcvia4 map to the existing nwell, via3 and via4 resistance rows. The two via values also apply to their MIM contact aliases, via3_cap and via4_cap.







Every dataset explicitly supplies all ten layer, four contact and five via rows. Missing values are errors; they do not inherit nominal resistance. Other sheet and cut values follow the reviewed extraction tables, with their units and source hashes recorded in the dataset provenance.






3.9.10.1 Understanding MIM Bounds


The published MIM specification gives RSCAPM as 5.8 \(\Omega/\square\), bounded by 4.8 and 6.8 \(\Omega/\square\), for both MIM top electrodes. These are the capm and capm2 sheet-resistance rows.


The -mim-bound selections pair the upper limit with high-R styles and the lower limit with low-R styles. This is an explicit engineering sensitivity policy. The specification does not establish that these limits occur together with the selected R/C model style. The component provenance records that assumption separately from the imported model parameters.


Keep the drawn polygons and contact count fixed when interpreting the result. For a rectangular sheet and \(N\) identical contacts in parallel, the material laws are


\[
R_{\mathrm{sheet}}=R_{\square}\frac{L}{W},
\qquad
R_{\mathrm{contacts}}=\frac{R_{\mathrm{cut}}}{N}.
\]


No compact-model linewidth shift is applied to the extracted sheet, and the actual cuts determine \(N\). The device models for capm and capm2 have their own effective-width and effective-length corrections and estimated contact counts. Applying those corrections again to the extraction geometry would change the meaning of this fixed-layout comparison.


These selections support analytical extraction with --2.5D. They do not specify a combined geometry/material worst case, a transistor corner, temperature, or a probability of the selected values occurring together. Their nominal stack supplies compatible layer identities and ordering; physical_stack_matches: false prevents exporting it as matched corner geometry. Automatic corner-specific device-capacitance checks are unavailable unless an independent reference is supplied explicitly.








3.9.10.2 Comparing Via Stacks


The example LVS database contains one cut at each connection from poly to met5, with ports at the cut centres and no intervening wire length. Download the sky130A catalog bundle and keep the layout unchanged for all five selections.


GDS: https://github.com/iic-jku/klayout-pex/blob/main/testdata/designs/sky130A/test_patterns/r_via_stack_1x1_minsize_poly_to_met5.gds.gz


unzip sky130A.zip
for corner in nominal hrhc-mim-bound hrlc-mim-bound \
    lrhc-mim-bound lrlc-mim-bound; do
  kpex extract --pdk sky130A --2.5D --mode R \
    --tech-catalog sky130A/catalog.pb.json --corner "$corner" \
    --lvsdb sky130-via-stack.lvsdb.gz \
    --out-dir "output/$corner" \
    --out-netlist "output/$corner.spice" \
    --out-result "output/$corner.json"
done


With hrhc-mim-bound, the written netlist contains these six physical-cut resistors:


Rext_2 li1 met1 23
Rext_3 li1 poly 252
Rext_4 met1 met2 15
Rext_5 met2 met3 8
Rext_6 met3 met4 6.623
Rext_7 met4 met5 0.7377















The full netlist also includes a dangling 0.001 \(\Omega\) tie from li1 to the original LVS net name, omitted from the excerpt and Figure 7. With the intermediate ports unloaded, this branch draws no current and the six physical resistances add in series:







The distinct high-R and low-R results come from via3 and via4, which depend on both R and C choices. This via stack demonstrates the source-dependent cut values; it does not establish correlation for MIM sheet bounds.










3.9.11 Matching Physical Geometry to Analytical Tables


Analytical extraction needs conductor ordering and connectivity from the stack, while its numerical capacitance comes from tables. A table-only corner can therefore use a nominal stack explicitly for structural purposes.


A field solver instead calculates capacitance from physical geometry and materials. Exporting nominal geometry under a nonnominal label would not reproduce a table corner. A scenario consequently declares whether its selected physical stack matches the scenario.







A missing capability produces a diagnostic before extraction. Device checks can instead use an explicitly supplied reference JSON file. Its physical assumptions remain the user’s choice. A nominal reference is never inherited automatically by a scenario that declares none.


The matching-stack declaration records a dataset contract, not foundry certification. It is checked before layout loading; availability of individual physical profiles is checked against the extracted shapes afterward. A numerical recipe may vary permittivity, thickness or manufactured width. Those choices require their own sources and must not be inferred from the spelling of a corner name.






3.9.11.1 Selecting Source Recipes


The development catalogs provide capiche-low-c and capiche-high-c for sky130A, gf180mcuD, ihp-sg13g2 and ihp-sg13cmos5l. These select the physical interconnect recipes from the pinned Capiche sources, together with the corresponding empirical C tables.







The source mapping relates the physical recipes to the extraction styles. The catalog records the separate source revisions for the physical recipe and empirical coefficients. This relationship does not make a finite 3D solve numerically identical to a fitted table, establish a correlated resistance corner, or constitute silicon calibration.


The R dataset deliberately stays nominal. These selections declare matching physical geometry within the supported profile scope, but no automatic device-capacitance reference. Unsupported MIM profiles are checked against the actual layout, as described in Section 3.9.11.5.







A source material named air is not necessarily vacuum. kpex pex25d preserves its declared permittivity. kpex extract --fastercap and --fastcap use --k-void instead, defaulting to 3.9. To retain the source background, select the value in Table 22.







Both extraction options use the shared PEX25DFile, PEX25DScene and scene exporter. Their electrostatic scope retains extracted diffusion and tap solids; kpex pex25d defaults to interconnect with device-terminal anchors. Background and domain settings can differ too. Compare exporters using the same prepared scene and solver settings.


The source substrate is an ideal 2D ground surface at \(z=0\). The 3D recipes retain a finite ground thickness as numerical truncation. sky130A also retains a 0.1 µm clearance below that surface, so a full ground plane does not touch device contacts beginning at \(z=0\). Its exported ground top is therefore \(z=-0.1\) µm. The gf180mcuD and ihp-sg13* recipes retain their existing zero clearance. The component provenance records this 3D boundary policy separately from the source geometry.








3.9.11.2 Applying Manufactured Width


MetalLayer.line_width_bias is the signed total change from drawn to manufactured width, in micrometres. If the drawn width is \(W\) and the bias is \(b\),


\[
W_{\mathrm{physical}}=W+b, \qquad
\Delta_{\mathrm{edge}}=\frac{b}{2}.
\]


Positive \(b\) grows metal; negative \(b\) erodes it. Every contour edge follows the same law, including line ends and holes. Growing metal reduces a hole; eroding metal enlarges it. Contact cuts retain their drawn shapes and positions.















The physical grid must represent the half-bias exactly. For example, the sky130A met1 change of \(-0.0206\) µm moves each boundary inward by \(0.0103\) µm: 103 units on a \(0.0001\) µm grid. A half-bias between grid points is rejected; kpex pex25d --grid can select a finer grid that also divides the layout DBU. Non-Manhattan polygon vertices are snapped to that grid, so their geometric displacement has a grid-sized discretization error.


The geometry must retain its electrical connections. Export stops if a bias:


    

  • Removes a conductor or separates an originally connected polygon
    • 

  • Breaks a contact, terminal or connection between touching conductor profiles
    • 

  • Joins different conductors, including a new boundary touch
    • 

  • Exceeds the native coordinate range
    • 



Touching profiles can require a joint physical recipe. Independently specified offsets that would open an internal seam are rejected, even when each profile remains nonempty. This avoids silently converting one conductor into disconnected pieces. Zero bias preserves drawn geometry.


These offsets apply to physical export. They do not resize polygons for analytical --2.5D extraction or replace its selected R/C coefficient tables.








3.9.11.3 Exporting the Same Layout


The example has two drawn 100 µm square plates: li1 from \((0,0)\) to \((100,100)\) µm, and met1 from \((50,50)\) to \((150,150)\) µm. Their drawn overlap is 50 µm square. Download the LVS database and the sky130A catalog bundle.


GDS: https://github.com/iic-jku/klayout-pex/blob/main/testdata/designs/sky130A/test_patterns/overlap_plates_100um_x_100um_li1_m1.gds.gz


mkdir -p catalogs
unzip sky130A.zip -d catalogs
for corner in capiche-low-c capiche-high-c; do
  kpex pex25d --pdk sky130A \
    --tech-catalog catalogs/sky130A/catalog.pb.json \
    --corner "$corner" --lvsdb overlap.lvsdb.gz \
    --grid 0.0001 --out-dir "output/$corner" \
    --out-file "output/$corner.pex25d" \
    --out-scene "output/$corner.pex25d.scene.pb"
done


The generated low-C file contains these layer extents:


METAL li1 Z_OFFSETS 1.177 1.257
METAL met1 Z_OFFSETS 1.7295 2.0595


The high-C file instead contains:


METAL li1 Z_OFFSETS 0.6917 0.8067
METAL met1 Z_OFFSETS 1.0137 1.4037







The gap is the met1 bottom minus the li1 top. Both the XY boundaries and the stack heights change; one global capacitance multiplier cannot describe this geometry. The resolved low-C scene and high-C scene are ready for a PEX25D exporter.








3.9.11.4 Comparing Finite Plates


A representative numerical check uses two aligned 10 µm square plates on the first and second routing-metal layers. It applies the selected manufactured widths, stack heights and dielectric constants, with an 8 µm field margin. The mutual capacitance is the average magnitude of the two off-diagonal matrix entries; substrate coupling is a different observable.


The independent area-only estimate is


\[
C_{\mathrm{area}}=\epsilon_0\epsilon_r\frac{W_{\mathrm{physical}}^2}{g},
\]


where \(g\) is the selected dielectric gap. Finite plates also have edge coupling, which this area law omits. Comparing the two exposes mistakes in units, gap, width or permittivity without treating the area law as an exact finite-geometry solution.


From a source checkout containing these recipes, the recorded cases can be reproduced with:


poetry run pytest tests/physical_corner_data_test.py::\
test_physical_corner_parallel_plates_converge_and_preserve_expected_order \
  -q -s


The recorded results and solver logs use KLayout module 0.30.13 and FasterCap 6.2.1. Each case was solved at tolerances 0.02 and 0.005; the 3D column gives the latter result.







The finite-plate results exceed the area estimates by 2.724–10.956%. Tightening the solver tolerance changes the mutual capacitance by at most 0.313% in magnitude. The high recipe gives a larger capacitance than low for every tested technology.


This validates representative physical dimensions, material assignment and numerical behavior. It does not establish agreement with the empirical analytical tables, qualify arbitrary layouts or provide silicon calibration. A fitted table also contains its own geometry conventions and finite-length assumptions.








3.9.11.5 Checking Available Profiles


A physical recipe may describe interconnect without supplying a qualified MIM corner law. A nominal MIM plate height or thickness retained for layer ordering is insufficient evidence for a nonnominal 3D model. MetalLayer.physical_geometry_unavailable makes that distinction explicit.


The source recipes mark these conductor profiles unavailable:







A layout containing an unavailable profile or a contact touching it is rejected before physical output is generated. If the layout contains neither, the profile, associated contacts and dependent conformal coatings are omitted from the exported physical model. A missing layout-layer mapping also fails, because absence could not be verified.


For example, download the MIM LVS database:


GDS: https://github.com/iic-jku/klayout-pex/blob/main/testdata/designs/sky130A/test_patterns/cap_mim_m3_20um_x_20um_over_m2_wire.gds.gz


kpex pex25d --pdk sky130A \
  --tech-catalog catalogs/sky130A/catalog.pb.json \
  --corner capiche-low-c --lvsdb mim.lvsdb.gz --blackbox n \
  --out-dir output/mim --out-file output/mim.pex25d


The run rejects the unsupported plate:


Could not generate PEX25D: Selected physical recipe has no
qualified geometry for 'capm', present on net 'B'


No output/mim.pex25d is produced. Selecting nominal is a separate comparison using the existing nominal geometry, not a substitute for the missing MIM corner. The missing evidence is a source-backed combination of MIM plate geometry, surrounding dielectric geometry and relevant dimensional changes for that corner.








3.9.11.6 Reading Coating Thicknesses


A conformal coating can wrap a metal or another coating. Its top and side thicknesses are incremental from the wrapped profile. Its field thickness is the total height from the bottom of the root metal, including any inner field coating. The latter is not added again along the chain.


The ihp-sg13cmos5l recipe illustrates the distinction. pass1 wraps TopMetal1; pass2 wraps pass1. Both reference the bottom of TopMetal1 for their field extents.




















TopMetal1 starts at \(z=5.4\) µm and is 2.0 µm thick. Over metal, the outer top is therefore \(5.4+2.0+1.5+0.4=9.3\) µm. Beside metal, the outer reach is \(0.3+0.3=0.6\) µm. In the field, the outer height is \(5.4+1.9=7.3\) µm.


Material precedence leaves pass1 in the lower 1.5 µm of the field and pass2 in the next 0.4 µm. Setting the pass2 field value to only 0.4 µm would hide it entirely beneath pass1. This error can be present even when no TopMetal1 shapes occur in the layout.


The low/high choices vary the relative permittivities of these coatings: pass1 uses 3.69/4.51 and pass2 uses 5.94/7.26. Their geometry above is unchanged. These values come from the low and high source recipes. Section 11.1.5.5 describes the corresponding WRAPS and material-precedence rules.










3.9.12 Selecting Device-Capacitance References


A capacitance component describes the extracted interconnect. A device-reference component supplies independent model expressions for --check-device-caps (Section 8.4). Selecting one does not select the other. The catalog must name the intended reference explicitly.


The additional reference components cover these MIM models:







For sky130A, the two mapped devices are:


    

  • sky130_fd_pr__model__cap_mim
    • 

  • sky130_fd_pr__model__cap_mim_m4
    • 



The references describe low-frequency mutual capacitance at zero bias and zero mismatch. The model reference temperatures are 27 °C for sky130A and ihp-sg13g2, and 25 °C for gf180mcuD. Series resistance, leakage and substrate shunts are separate observables.


The source equations are checked against pinned compact-model simulations. For a two-terminal device, the mutual capacitance follows the off-diagonal admittance:


\[
C_{AB}=-\frac{\operatorname{Im}Y_{AB}}{\omega}.
\]


The comparison uses frequencies low enough that series resistance does not materially change this observable. It does not interpret leakage conductance as capacitance or compare the sum of all capacitances attached to a net.




3.9.12.1 Preserving the Model’s Corner Law


Different models vary different terms:


    

  • sky130A: the R/C style changes the effective dimensions as well as area and edge coefficients. Two styles with the same C suffix can therefore require different reference expressions
    • 

  • gf180mcuD: the supported 2 fF MIM option scales both area and perimeter terms by its own MIM corner parameter
    • 

  • ihp-sg13g2: cap_cmim varies its area density while retaining the literal edge density of \(40\,\mathrm{aF}/\mu\mathrm m\). Its multiplier applies once to the complete device capacitance
    • 



For the IHP reference, with mapped dimensions expressed in micrometres,


\[
C_{\mathrm{reference}}=m\left[C_AWL+2C_P(W+L)\right].
\]


The low and high components use \(C_A=1.35\) and \(1.65\,\mathrm{fF}/\mu\mathrm m^2\), respectively, while \(C_P=0.04\,\mathrm{fF}/\mu\mathrm m\) stays fixed. A global multiplier applied to nominal capacitance would incorrectly change that edge term too.








3.9.12.2 Comparing MIM Plates at Two Capacitance Selections


The complete MIM comparison catalog declares mim-low-c and mim-high-c. They pair the corresponding C tables and device-reference component while holding resistance nominal. This is an explicitly authored sensitivity comparison, without a claim of correlated resistance or matching field-solver geometry.


The low selection contains:


{
  "id": "mim-low-c",
  "resistance": "nominal",
  "capacitance": "low",
  "process_stack": "nominal",
  "device_references": "low",
  "physical_stack_matches": false
}


The high selection names high for both capacitance and device references. Neither selection inherits the nominal MOM references.


GDS: https://github.com/iic-jku/klayout-pex/blob/main/testdata/designs/ihp-sg13g2/test_patterns/cap_cmim_20um_x_20um_over_m4_wire.gds.gz


The layout contains a 20 µm × 20 µm cap_cmim with terminals A ↔︎ B, above a separate Metal4 route. Set KPEX_DIR to the source checkout, then run:


unzip ihp-mim-reference.zip
pattern=cap_cmim_20um_x_20um_over_m4_wire
layouts="$KPEX_DIR/testdata/designs/ihp-sg13g2/test_patterns"
lvsdbs="$KPEX_DIR/testdata/lvsdb/ihp-sg13g2/test_patterns"
for corner in mim-low-c mim-high-c; do
  kpex extract --pdk ihp-sg13g2 --2.5D --mode CC \
    --blackbox y --halo 8 --scale y \
    --gds "$layouts/$pattern.gds.gz" \
    --lvsdb "$lvsdbs/$pattern.lvsdb.gz" \
    --tech-catalog ihp-mim-reference/catalog.pb.json \
    --corner "$corner" --check-device-caps \
    --out-dir "output/$corner" \
    --out-result "output/$corner.json"
done












In this LVS definition, both device-owned plates stop at the MIM rectangle. The lower electrode’s 2 µm overhang is ordinary Metal5, outside that ownership region. The marker observer therefore excludes fringe coupling to the overhang and reports area coupling only, while the model includes its 3.2 fF perimeter contribution.


The separate route’s coupling is also outside this device-local comparison. Both results are informational: no acceptance bound was supplied. Their ratios compare different observation domains and must not be interpreted as qualification of the complete device capacitance.






3.9.12.3 Limits of Device-Corner References


The components cover only the listed MIM models. MOM devices, RF MIM models, other MIM density options and unlisted capacitor types remain unchecked. A layout with no supported references fails a requested automatic check with an explanation.


The existing nominal reference component is unchanged. In particular, the IHP nominal MOM engineering estimates remain available under their original assumptions; the new MIM components do not supply nonnominal MOM laws or automatically add nominal MIM checks.


The selected expressions reject nonpositive effective dimensions and invalid multiplicities. They do not replace PDK layout rules, qualify arbitrary bias or temperature, or define statistical correlations with transistor corners. A custom explicit reference file remains available when another independently justified comparison is needed.










3.9.13 Recording What Was Used


kpex_result.json, or the path selected by --out-result, records technology_selection:


    

  • Technology and scenario identifiers
    • 

  • Catalog path and SHA256 of its exact bytes
    • 

  • Catalog description, structured provenance and data revision
    • 

  • Selected component identifiers, content hashes, source records, assumptions and revision histories
    • 

  • Hash of the complete selected input technology
    • 

  • Whether a matching physical stack and device references were declared
    • 



Sources, source references and revision history are validated before using the selected data. A missing source identity, unknown source identifier, invalid calendar date or inconsistent current revision is an error.


Each component file is checked against the catalog’s byte hash. Changing or reformatting a file while retaining an old byte hash is detected. A byte-identical copy retains the same hash. The resolved content identities are separate: irrelevant JSON object-key order does not change the identity, while physically significant stack and terminal order is retained.


technology_selection.resolved_technology_sha256 identifies the selected input before runtime overrides. An extraction with --halo 3 records its effective halo separately as halo_um, and preserves the override in arguments. Keep the complete result with the netlist rather than using a scenario label alone as a reproducibility key.


PEX25D metadata records the selected process_corner. Physical-stack identity remains distinct from the capacitance-table identity, which matters when comparing geometry generation with fitted or imported coefficients.






3.9.14 Limits


    

  • Explicit --corner or --tech-catalog cannot be combined with --magic, whose installed technology and extraction style are selected independently
    • 

  • A different conductor topology or layout/LVS interface needs a separate technology catalog
    • 

  • No voltage, temperature, statistical variation or transistor-model selection is inferred
    • 

  • An analytical corner without a matching physical recipe cannot be exported as corner-matched solver geometry
    • 

  • Only the scenarios declared by the supplied catalog can be selected
    • 













4 KPEX/FasterCap Engine


FasterCap is a 3D and 2D parallel capacitance field solver, inspired by FastCap2. The maintained fork is iic-jku/FasterCap.


Starting from an input layout (e.g. GDS file) and a process stack-up (part of the Section 3.3), KPEX creates input geometries for FasterCap. After running FasterCap, the Maxwell capacitance matrix is parsed and interpreted to obtain the parasitic capacitances.


See Section 2.4 to get started with a first extraction example.









4.1 3D Input Geometries







The FasterCap input files and their format are documented in the PDF manual (Di Lorenzo 2019).


KPEX generates 3D input geometries:


    

  • *.lst file: Main input file

      

    • defines dielectric instances
      • 

    • defines conductor instances
      • 

    • each instance refers to a *.geo file
      • 

    • 

  • *.geo files: Defines single geometry

      

    • defines shapes (e.g. triangles)
      • 

    • Each shape has a reference point to define inside/outsides
      • 

    • 












4.2 Example: MOM Capacitor







Figure 11 depicts the MOM capacitor from Section 2.4.


The corresponding schematic representation of Figure 12 contains 3 conductors (\(N_1\), \(N_2\) and \(N_3\)), and coupling capacitances:


    

  • Capacitances between conductors: \(C_{ij} \text{ where } i \ne j\)

      

    • \(C_{23}\) is the capacitance “intended” by the MOM designer
      • 

    • 

  • Capacitances between conductors and ground: \(C_{ii}\)
    • 




















4.3 Output Maxwell Capacitance Matrix


A Maxwell capacitance matrix (Maxwell 1873) provides the relation between voltages on a set of conductors and the charges on these conductors, as described by the FasterCap author in the white paper (Di Lorenzo 2023).


FasterCap log output prints the Maxwell capacitance matrix (one for each iteration/refinement).







    

  • Matrix Properties:

      

    • Scaling: units have to be divided by \(10^{-6}\)
      • 

    • rows and columns are the same (list of net names)
      • 

    • Row Cells:

        

      • off diagonals cells contains the coupling between row/col nets (times \(-1\))
        • 

      • diagonal cells contains the sum of the absolute values of all other cells in the row
        • 

      • 

    • Matrix Symmetry:

        

      • in theory (ideal world), the matrix would be symmetric
        • 

      • in practice it’s not
        

        • 

      • therefore FastCap2 did average the off-diagonals
        • 

      • FasterCap does not average, so it’s done as part of KPEX
        • 

      • 

    • 
















5 KPEX/MAGIC Engine


This engine is merely just a wrapper around magic, which prepares a TCL script that opens the layout file and starts MAGIC’s PEX flow. See Section 2.5 to get started with a first extraction example.


The following chapter will illustrate concepts of the parasitic extraction done in MAGIC, also motivated by the fact that the engine in Section 6 will be based on those. Major parts of this illustration, the figures and concepts are based on work done by MAGIC maintainer Tim Edwards, especially his talk from FSiC conference 2022 (Edwards 2022) and a (conceptual follow-up) ChipsAlliance meeting on April 4, 2023, see (Edwards 2023b) and (Edwards 2023a). In addition, code review and debugging of the MAGIC codebase was performed.




5.1 MAGIC database units


    

  • To convert between MAGIC database units and \(\mu m\), a scaling factor \(\alpha\) is used, so that \(L_{\mu m} = \frac{L_{dbu}}{\alpha}\)
    • 

  • E.g. for sky130A, \(\alpha = 200.0\)
    • 







5.2 Types of Parasitic Capacitances


MAGIC models multiple types of capacitances:


    

  • Substrate Overlap: Overlap area of a metal with the substrate
    • 

  • Substrate Fringing: Sidewall of a metal fringes out to substrate
    • 

  • Sidewall Capacitance: Coupling between adjacent sidewalls on the same layer
    • 

  • Overlap Capacitance: Overlap on different metal layers
    • 

  • Fringe Capacitance (“Side Overlap”): Sidewall of a metal fringes out other metal layers
    • 







5.3 Substrate Capacitance




    

  • Overlapping area: \[
C_{area} = \frac{\epsilon_{si} * K}{d} * \text{area} \,\,\,\,\,\,\, \left[ \frac{F}{\mu m^2} * \mu m^2\right]
\]
    • 

  • Fringe (“Perimeter”): \[
C_{fringe\,to\,substrate} = \text{perimeter} * C_{perim} = (2l + 2w)*C_{perim}
\]
    • 

  • Coefficients like \(C_{perim}\) are part of the tech files (Parasitic Tables)
    • 







5.4 Sidewall Capacitance




\[
C_{sidewall} = \frac{\epsilon_{si} * K}{s} * \text{sidewall area}  \,\,\,\,\,\,\, \left[ \frac{F}{\mu m^2} * \mu m^2\right]
\] \[
\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,= \frac{\epsilon_{si} * K}{s} * t * l  \,\,\,\,\,\,\, \left[ \frac{F}{\mu m^2} * \mu m * \mu m\right]
\] \[
C_{sidewall} = \frac{C_{sidewall\,coeff}}{s} * l \,\,\,\,\,\,\, \left[ \frac{F}{\mu m} * \mu m\right]
\]


The coefficient describes the coupling between the two facing sidewalls, but MAGIC walks every edge, so each of the two edges contributes half of it:


\[
C_{sidewall\,per\,edge} = \frac{1}{2} * \frac{C_{sidewall\,coeff}}{s} * l
\]




    

  • Coefficients are part of the tech files (Parasitic Tables)
    • 

  • Layer thickness \(t\) is normally multiplied into the coefficient
    • 

  • Foundry tables give constant coefficient referenced to \(s = 1\)
    • 















WarningCount the sidewall pair once







The sidewall coefficient describes the full pair. Half belongs to each directed edge visit. A second halving of the already weighted coefficient makes the pair too small by a factor of two.


MAGIC 8.3.693 removes that extra halving during final technology processing. The earlier interpretation that revisions before 8.3.679 simply counted the pair twice was incorrect. The upstream correction explains the two sites that applied the factor.


KPEX 0.9.0 restores the full pair value for both constant and sloped gaps. Updating the physical coefficient tables is a separate change: multiplying all extraction results by two would also alter overlap and fringe contributions, which are not affected by this counting correction.










5.5 Overlap Capacitance


    

  • Overlapping area: \[
C_{area} = \frac{\epsilon_{si} * K}{d} * \text{area} \,\,\,\,\,\,\, \left[ \frac{F}{\mu m^2} * \mu m^2\right]
\]
    • 












5.6 Fringe Capacitance







    

  • Causing sidewall (its bottom edge depicted red)
    • 

  • Assume: Field is bounded by fringe halo (e.g. \(8\, \mu m\) away from edge)
    • 

  • Fractions of fringe goes to metal1 or substrate
    • 








    

  • Multiplier \(\alpha\) (comes from tech files: overlap table)

      

    • determines how quickly fringe capacitance drops with increasing distance
      • 

    • \(\alpha\) is related to distance \(d\) between layers
      • 

    • \(\alpha\) is proportional to \(C_{overlap_{metal1 \leftrightarrow metal2}}= \frac{\epsilon_{si} * K}{d} * \text{area}\)
      
(for fixed value of area \(1\, \mu m^2\)) 
      • 

    • 

  • Fringe Fractions:

      

    • \(\text{frac}_{metal1} = \tfrac{2}{\pi} * \text{atan}(\alpha_{metal2 \rightarrow metal1}*x)\)
      • 

    • \(\text{frac}_{sub} = \tfrac{2}{\pi} * \text{atan}(\alpha_{metal2 \rightarrow sub}*(\text{halo}-x))\)
      • 

    • \(\tfrac{2}{\pi}\) is multiplied because of scaling to interval \([0.0,\,1.0]\), as \(\text{atan}(\infty)=\tfrac{\pi}{2}\)
      • 

    • 

  • Overlap capacitance:

      

    • \(C_{overlap} = \frac{\epsilon_{si} * K}{d} * \text{area} \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,(\text{with area}=1 \mu m^2)\)
      • 

    • 

  • Coupling capacitance \(metal1 \leftrightarrow metal2\):

      

    • \(\alpha_{metal1 \leftrightarrow metal2} = \alpha_{scalefac} * C_{overlap_{metal1 \leftrightarrow metal2}}\)
      • 

    • \(\text{frac}_{metal1} = \tfrac{2}{\pi} * \text{atan}(\alpha_{metal1 \leftrightarrow metal2}*x)\)
      • 

    • \(\text{effective length} = \text{edge length} * \text{frac}_{metal1}\)
      • 

    • \(C_{fringe_{metal2 \rightarrow metal1}} = \text{effective length} * C_{sideoverlap_{metal2 \rightarrow metal1}}\)
      • 

    • 

  • Coupling capacitance \(metal1 \leftrightarrow sub\):

      

    • \(\alpha_{metal1 \leftrightarrow sub} = \alpha_{scalefac} * C_{overlap_{metal1 \leftrightarrow sub}}\)
      • 

    • \(\text{frac}_{sub} = \tfrac{2}{\pi} * \text{atan}(\alpha_{metal1 \leftrightarrow sub}*(\text{halo}-x))\)
      • 

    • \(\text{effective length} = \text{edge length} * \text{frac}_{sub}\)
      • 

    • \(C_{fringe_{metal2 \rightarrow sub}} = \text{effective length} * C_{sideoverlap_{metal2 \rightarrow sub}}\)
      • 

    • 








    

  • Partial side overlap

      

    • In case there is only a partial side overlap, the non-existing near fraction is subtracted from the far fraction
      •
