    • \(metal1\) wire is offset, starts at \(x_{near}\)
      • 

    • \(metal1\) ends at \(x_{far}\)
      • 

    • 








    

  • \(\text{frac}_{near} = \tfrac{2}{\pi} * \text{atan}(\alpha*x_{near})\)
    • 

  • \(\text{frac}_{far} = \tfrac{2}{\pi} * \text{atan}(\alpha*x_{far})\)
    • 

  • \(\text{frac} = \text{frac}_{far}-\text{frac}_{near}\)
    • 







5.7 Shielding Effects












Note, given an analyzed sidewall (edge in 2D), lateral fringe shielding


    

  • is caused by opposing shapes on the same layer

      

    • even by the same polygon
      • 

    • by other polygons (same net)
      • 

    • by other polygons (different net) — this is what we also look at when analyzing sidewall coupling
      • 

    • 

  • will shield the fringing to the lower layers, i.e. in Figure 14 the coupling between the two shapes is the same in the above and below cases
    • 












5.8 Parasitic Resistance


Magic constructs a graph of resistors between nodes


    

  • device terminals
    • 

  • pins
    • 

  • junctions (vias or branching on the same metal layer)
    • 









5.8.1 Wire resistance


    

  • Given a wire with length \(l\) and height \(h\), the basic formula is \[
R_{wire} = \frac{l}{h} * R_{coeff}  \,\,\,\,\,\,\, \left[ \frac{\mu m}{\mu m} * mΩ\right]
\]
    • 

  • Coefficient \(R_{coeff}\) is part of the tech files (Parasitic Tables)
    

      

    • defined for every metal layer
      • 

    • in \(mΩ\) for \(1\,{\mu m}^2\)
      • 

    • Coefficient already includes the thickness aspect of the layer, so the formula works in 2D
      • 

    • 







5.8.2 Via resistance







    

  • Given

      

    • drawn via in the layout, with width \(w\) and height \(h\)
      • 

    • design rules defined for each via layer:

        

      • via width \(viawidth\)
        • 

      • \(spacing\) between vias (in case of a via array)
        • 

      • \(border\) on each side of the via
        • 

      • 

    • 

  • MAGIC interpretation of the via drawing

      

    • determine number of vias in \(x\) and \(y\) direction, i.e. \(n_x\) and \(n_y\)
      • 

    • if \(x\) and \(y\) dimensions are below the minimum size, MAGIC counts 1 via in each direction
      • 

    • if the dimensions are larger, we calculate how much vias fit
      • 

    • 



\[
R_{via} = \frac{R_{coeff}}{n_x * n_y}   \,\,\,\,\,\,\, \left[\frac{mΩ}{\text{via count}}\right]
\]


\[
n_x = 1 + \left\lfloor\frac{w - (viawidth + 2 * border)}{viawidth + spacing}\right\rfloor
\]


\[
n_y = 1 + \left\lfloor\frac{h - (viawidth + 2 * border)}{viawidth + spacing}\right\rfloor
\]


    

  • Coefficient \(R_{coeff}\) is part of the tech files (Parasitic Tables)

      

    • defined for every via layer
      • 

    • in \(mΩ\) per via
      • 

    • Coefficient already includes the thickness aspect of the layer, so the formula works in 2D
      • 

    • 













6 KPEX/2.5D Engine


This analytical extraction engine is separate from the PEX25D interchange format described in Section 11.1. kpex extract --2.5D selects the engine; kpex pex25d generates a geometry and material description without running an engine.


Field solvers are precise, yet slow, they are useful to obtain a golden reference.


For most use cases, a faster engine is desirable. KPEX/MAGIC is such an engine, but the MAGIC code is tightly coupled with the database, layer/via design choices, and user interface of MAGIC. For example, it runs single-threaded.


Therefore, the KPEX 2.5D Engine intends to implement the concepts and formulas of MAGIC (see Section 5.2), but in a way that is best suited to the KLayout API, and is modular and open for parallel execution.







In Figure 16, we see that as in the KPEX/FasterCap engine (see Section 4), a “LVS” script is used to extract the connectivity information and create an LVS report database.


As mentioned in Section 1.4, KPEX uses the KLayout API. During the course of this project, in cooperation with Matthias Köfferlein, the KLayout API was extended, in order to simplify parasitic extraction.


The engine uses those new API classes to extract parasitic capacitances:


    

  • klayout.db.PolygonNeighborhoodVisitor (since 0.30.1): used during the extraction of overlap capacitances (see Section 5.5)
    • 

  • klayout.db.EdgeNeighborhoodVisitor (since 0.30.1): used during the extraction of sidewall capacitances (see Section 5.4) and fringe capacitances (see Section 5.6)
    • 

  • Geometry classes with properties in klayout.db (since 0.30.1): store net information directly on polygons, edges, edge pairs and boxes
    • 



The engine uses those new API classes to extract parasitic resistances:


    

  • klayout.pex module (since KLayout 0.30.2)

      

    • klayout.pex.RNetExtractor: used to extract resistance networks
      • 

    • klayout.pex.RExtractorTech: minimal process stack description for conductor and via layers
      • 

    • 





6.1 Choosing the Level of Detail


--mode CC keeps each connected net equipotential. --mode R breaks its conductors into a resistance network. --mode RC places extracted capacitances on that distributed network as well, so the position of a load along a wire affects the simulated response.


Grounded capacitance is an explicit approximation: --mode C uses ideal conductors, while --mode RC --coupling grounded retains distributed resistance. The development-version options, floating-conductor treatment and standalone postprocessing are described in Section 7.


The capacitance model has separate area-overlap, facing-sidewall and fringe terms. Polygon integration preserves their geometric meaning for sloped boundaries (Section 6.2). It does not turn the analytical model into a field solver or remove the need to check its coefficients against the intended technology.


The halo limits which neighboring geometry participates in sidewall and fringe extraction. Keep the same halo and fringe normalization when comparing runs. Recent neighborhood batching and rectangular-shield interval subtraction reduce repeated geometric work while retaining the polygon path for general shapes. They do not justify shrinking the halo to obtain a faster result.






6.2 Capacitance of Sloped and Holed Polygons


A wire does not have to end in a rectangle. A taper, a diagonal segment, or a shield with a hole changes the distance to the neighboring conductor along the edge. KPEX/2.5D integrates that changing geometry using the same overlap, sidewall, and fringe models introduced in Section 5.2.


This extends where those models can be applied. It does not turn the analytical extraction into a three-dimensional field solution: the dielectric stack and fitted parasitic coefficients still determine the model’s accuracy.




6.2.1 Looking Along One Edge


For each source edge, imagine rotating the layout until that edge lies on the horizontal axis. Let \(x\) run along the edge and \(y\) point outwards from its conductor. The local coordinate system is attached to the edge, so a diagonal wire needs no special capacitance formula.


The neighborhood is divided into intervals where the facing boundaries remain straight. Within one interval:


    

  • A sidewall gap is a linear function \(d(x)\)
    • 

  • A fringe target has a near boundary \(n(x)\) and a far boundary \(f(x)\)
    • 

  • A shield can shorten either boundary or remove a part of the target
    • 
















A bounding box loses this information. It fills the empty space beside a triangle and across a hole. Using the minimum distance everywhere also assigns the closest part’s stronger coupling to the whole edge.


Overlap capacitance needs no distance integration in this plane. It is proportional to the actual unshielded intersection area, including the subtraction of holes:


\[
C_{\mathrm{overlap}} = \frac{k_{\mathrm{ov}}}{1000}\,A_{\mathrm{visible}}.
\]


Here \(k_{\mathrm{ov}}\) is in \(\mathrm{aF}/\mu\mathrm{m}^2\), area is in \(\mu\mathrm{m}^2\), and the result is in \(\mathrm{fF}\).






6.2.2 Integrating a Changing Sidewall Gap


Take an edge interval of length \(L\) with endpoint gaps \(d_0\) and \(d_1\):


\[
d(x)=d_0+\frac{d_1-d_0}{L}\,x,\qquad 0\leq x\leq L.
\]


The technology fit adds an offset \(o\) to the physical gap. For a positive physical gap, a negative offset must not make the fitted separation zero or negative. KPEX/2.5D therefore uses


\[
s(d)=\max\left(d+o,\frac d2\right).
\]


The geometry factor is the integral of the reciprocal separation:


\[
G_{\mathrm{sw}}=\int_0^L \frac{dx}{s(d(x))}.
\]


For a full-pair sidewall coefficient \(k_{\mathrm{sw}}\) in \(\mathrm{aF}\), one directed edge contributes


\[
C_{\mathrm{sw,edge}}=\frac{k_{\mathrm{sw}}G_{\mathrm{sw}}}{2\cdot1000}
\quad [\mathrm{fF}].
\]


The two directed visits together count the pair once. The geometry integral introduces no additional half, and the conversion from \(\mathrm{aF}\) to \(\mathrm{fF}\) divides by \(1000\). This counting convention is separate from the shape of the gap (Section 5.4).


If the whole interval uses \(s=d+o\), the integral has a closed form:


\[
G_{\mathrm{sw}}=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle \frac{L}{d_0+o}, & d_0=d_1,\\[8pt]
\displaystyle \frac{L}{d_1-d_0}
\ln\left(\frac{d_1+o}{d_0+o}\right), & d_0\ne d_1.
\end{cases}
\]


The logarithm is the result of integrating \(1/(a+bx)\). It is not a correction fitted specifically to diagonal wires. Reversing the edge exchanges \(d_0\) and \(d_1\) and changes both signs, leaving the result unchanged.


For a negative \(o\), the two separation branches meet at \(d=-2o\). If a taper crosses that gap, split its integral there. On the clamped part, integrate \(2/d\) instead of \(1/(d+o)\). The two branches agree at the split, so no capacitance jump is introduced.




6.2.2.1 Why the Mean Gap Is Insufficient


Consider \(L=4\,\mu\mathrm{m}\), a gap widening from \(0.2\) to \(0.6\,\mu\mathrm{m}\), and \(o=0.1\,\mu\mathrm{m}\). These values describe a geometry exercise, independently of any PDK coefficient:


\[
G_{\mathrm{sw}}=
\frac{4}{0.6-0.2}\ln\left(\frac{0.6+0.1}{0.2+0.1}\right)
=10\ln(7/3).
\]


Replacing the taper by its mean gap gives \(4/(0.4+0.1)=8\). The integral is larger because reducing a small gap strengthens coupling more than increasing an already large gap weakens it.


The first half of the edge carries the fraction


\[
\frac{C_{[0,L/2]}}{C_{[0,L]}}
=\frac{\ln(5/3)}{\ln(7/3)},
\]


which is greater than one half. This matters when the capacitance is assigned to different nodes of an extracted resistor network.








6.2.3 Integrating Fringe Across a Target


The fringe model uses a cumulative fraction


\[
F(y)=\frac{2}{\pi}\arctan\bigl(\alpha\max(0,y)\bigr).
\]


\(F(y)\) describes how much of the fringe is reached by distance \(y\). Its slope decreases with distance. A strip near the source edge therefore receives more fringe than an equally wide strip farther away.


For a strip extending from \(n(x)\) to \(f(x)\), the received fraction is \(F(f(x))-F(n(x))\). Integrating along the source edge gives


\[
C_{\mathrm{fringe}}=
\frac{k_{\mathrm{fr}}}{1000\,N}
\int_0^L \left[F(f(x))-F(n(x))\right]dx.
\]


\(k_{\mathrm{fr}}\) is the directional side-overlap coefficient in \(\mathrm{aF}/\mu\mathrm{m}\). \(N\) describes halo normalization, explained below. The overlap table supplies the parameter \(\alpha\) for this source/target layer pair, while the side-overlap table supplies \(k_{\mathrm{fr}}\). They play different roles: one sets the distance dependence, the other its magnitude.


In the current coefficient convention, the numerical value of \(\alpha\) in \(\mu\mathrm{m}^{-1}\) is \(0.02\) times the overlap coefficient in \(\mathrm{aF}/\mu\mathrm{m}^2\). This scaling belongs to the empirical fringe model; it is not an identity between capacitance and inverse distance.















The near and far boundaries of a trapezoid are linear functions. Their integrals can be evaluated analytically using


\[
J(z)=z\arctan(z)-\frac12\ln(1+z^2),
\qquad J'(z)=\arctan(z).
\]


For \(q(x)=q_0+mx>0\), \(m\ne0\) and \(\alpha>0\):


\[
\int_a^b F(q(x))\,dx
=\frac{2}{\pi\alpha m}
\left[J(\alpha q(b))-J(\alpha q(a))\right].
\]


A constant boundary gives \((b-a)F(q_0)\). A boundary crossing zero is split there, because the part behind the source edge contributes no outward fringe. The implementation evaluates equivalent forms that avoid subtracting nearly equal numbers when the slope or \(\alpha\) is small.






6.2.4 Subtracting Shields and Keeping Holes


A nearer conductor on the same layer limits the lateral reach. Its sloping facing edge produces a sloping shadow, rather than a rectangle beginning at one mean distance. This shadow also applies when the nearby shape belongs to the same net or to the opposite side of the same polygon.


For a target on a different layer, conductors between the source and target provide additional shielding. The source-to-target ordering matters: a conductor beyond the target does not shield that target. Above and below the source are handled separately.


After subtracting these shields, a target may be concave or have holes. KPEX/2.5D partitions the remaining geometry into vertical trapezoids in the source edge’s local coordinates:


    

  1. Split at the distinct horizontal positions of polygon vertices
    2. 

  2. Find the boundary crossings within each strip
    3. 

  3. Pair successive crossings as filled intervals, leaving holes empty
    4. 

  4. Integrate each trapezoid and add its contribution
    5. 
















This is a partition of the visible polygon, not a replacement by rectangles. Intersections at a new strip boundary remain floating-point values for the capacitance calculation. Only the geometry drawn in the extraction report is rounded back onto the layout grid.


The small-contribution cutoff is applied to each resulting unshielded polygon before its internal trapezoids are emitted. A polygon that contributes more than \(0.0001\,\mathrm{fF}\) remains even if each trapezoid individually contributes less. A value equal to the cutoff is omitted. Changing the mathematical subdivision therefore does not change whether that polygon is retained.






6.2.5 Preserving the Profile When Geometry Is Cut


The total capacitance is not enough when a marker removes part of an edge or when RC extraction divides it between nodes. The taper example above has equal lengths on either side of its midpoint but unequal capacitances.


KPEX/2.5D retains an integral profile for a sloped contribution. A cut asks the profile for the capacitance over the retained interval. A later cut uses the original coordinates of that interval. It does not restart the distance ramp at its new left endpoint.


This makes three operations consistent:


    

  • Summing the parts reproduces the original contribution before cutoffs
    • 

  • An exclusion marker removes the capacitance carried by its covered geometry
    • 

  • RC node assignment uses the local capacitance density, rather than only the fraction of edge length
    • 



For overlap capacitance, the density within one layer pair is uniform per area, so area fractions remain appropriate.






6.2.6 Inspecting Sloped Wires


The sky130A pattern below has a tapered conductor A, a bent conductor B, and a rectangular conductor C. The A ↔︎ B gap varies along the taper, whereas part of the B ↔︎ C gap is constant.


GDS: sidewall_non_parallel_li1.gds.gz















From the klayout-pex source checkout, the committed LVS database allows the extraction to be repeated without running LVS:


lvsdb_dir=testdata/lvsdb/sky130A/test_patterns
kpex extract --pdk sky130A --mode CC --blackbox n \
  --lvsdb "$lvsdb_dir/sidewall_non_parallel_li1.lvsdb.gz" \
  --2.5D --halo 8 --scale y --report-caps y \
  --out-dir output_polygon_example


The example was checked with klayout-pex 0.9.0 and the KLayout Python module 0.30.13. --report-caps y adds each contribution and its geometry to the extraction report. Inspect the A ↔︎ B sidewall entries to see how the facing intervals follow the taper. The exported netlist combines the contributions belonging to the same pair of nets.






6.2.7 Halo, Grid and Model Limits


The halo is the finite lateral neighborhood searched around an edge. --halo overrides the technology’s side_halo, in \(\mu\mathrm{m}\). It changes which geometry is considered, so it is a modeling choice as well as a runtime limit.


The default --scale y normalizes the fringe fraction to that halo. For a positive overlap coefficient and halo \(h\), \(N=F(h)\), and a target occupying the full interval from \(0\) to \(h\) receives the full coefficient for that edge length. A zero overlap coefficient gives \(\alpha=0\) and zero fringe contribution before normalization. With --scale n, \(N=1\), so the tail beyond the halo remains omitted. A larger halo can change both the visible targets and, when scaling is enabled, the normalization of nearer ones.


The --scale flag here concerns fringe fractions. It is independent of SPICE .option scale, which controls the interpretation of selected device geometry parameters.


These limits matter when comparing results:


    

  • An overlap coefficient of exactly zero gives zero fringe, including with halo scaling enabled
    • 

  • Very small positive overlap coefficients approach a uniform distribution across a normalized halo
    • 

  • Rotating a layout onto an integer grid can move vertices and neighborhood boundaries slightly
    • 

  • Intervals no longer than one database unit are discarded to suppress degenerate edge neighborhoods
    • 

  • The analytical model does not resolve full three-dimensional corner fields or replace coefficient calibration
    • 



For a rotation comparison, keep the same physical dimensions, coefficient tables, halo, and scaling option. A finer database unit reduces geometric rounding. Quarter-turn rotations preserve integer-grid coordinates exactly; arbitrary angles usually do not.








6.3 Excluding Parts of the Layout


Some structures are better served by a model than by a 2.5D extraction: an inductor by an EM simulation, which also has its inductance, a hard block by a netlist of its own, or the power grid of a block by the extraction of the top level. FEM co-simulation for example matches measured mm-wave amplifiers better than an RC extraction (Sagouo Minko and Stander 2019). The rest of the layout should still be extracted, and connect to the model.


This raises four questions, which this section answers:


    

  • How does a layout say what the extraction should leave out, and for which layers?
    • 

  • What happens to the shapes there: can they just be removed, with dielectric in their place?
    • 

  • What about the capacitances between what is left out and what is not?
    • 

  • How does the rest of the layout connect to the model?
    • 



There are three ways to select what is left out, which follow the same rule (Section 6.3.3):







By default, nothing is left out, so that a netlist doesn’t change without one of these. Markers and cells are read from the GDS, so that these options need --gds, also together with --lvsdb, as an LVS database only has the shapes of nets.


The options work with --2.5D, --fastercap and --fastcap (Section 6.3.9), not with --magic.




6.3.1 What the PDKs Mark







The layer rules of the IHP PDKs don’t describe the markers beyond one line each. What the pair markers can mean follows from their names, as they name a pair of plates. Of the 533 GDS of the IHP reference layouts and LVS testcases, 25 have a marker, all of them noqrc of rfcmim.


By default, KPEX honors NoRCX.drawing and the pair markers. noqrc only takes effect on request, with --exclusion-marker-layer (Section 6.3.6): the extraction of the rfcmim already knows the device, in white-box mode it would lose the capacitor, and in a reference layout it would hit 2624 µm² of metal that isn’t part of the device.


sky130A and gf180mcuD have no layer for this, in their layer tables or in the cells and layouts looked at. SkyWater’s extraction rules leave parasitics to the models by device recognition (varactors, MIM capacitors, RF ESD diodes, precision poly resistors), and MAGIC by the property device of a cell, which zeroes the parasitics of the cell. So these PDKs take markers of the user (Section 6.3.6).






6.3.2 Why the Geometry Stays


Tools take one of three approaches, here by the public material of commercial tools:







Removing the shapes is the simple approach, but it changes what is outside them, as Figure 21 shows. A 2.5D extraction rests on the shielding by what is in between: neighbors reduce the coupling across a layer from 16.3 % to 1.8 % of the total, and it’s only negligible above a metal density threshold (Cong et al. 1997). The same holds for metal without a function: ignoring dummy fill gives errors above 30 %, and the fill on other layers matters more than the fill on the same layer (Kurokawa et al. 2004). Full-chip extractors handle grounded fill, floating fill needs a 3D solver (Kahng et al. 2006; Yu et al. 2006).







Table 33 has this for small layouts of ihp-sg13g2, in --mode CC, with FasterCap in brackets. FasterCap is no reference here, it only shows the same trend. “Coupling dropped” keeps the shape as a shield, but leaves out all of its capacitances, also those to the wires.







So the shapes stay: without them, the wires around them have wrong values, which neither the netlist nor the model can correct.












Note







With a marker over all layers, the parts of A and B within it are left out too, so the first rows of Table 33 apply to a neighbor like N, and to the parts near the edge of the marker. They apply fully where only some shapes are left out at a location: a marker of one layer (Section 6.3.6), a cell with routing over it (Section 6.3.7), or a net (Section 6.3.8).






The coil of a PDK inductor is an exception that does no harm: the deck of KPEX takes the metal within IND out of the conductors, so that it is no shield, but it is 30 µm from the edge of its polygon, beyond the halo of 8 µm, so that nothing outside the polygon is affected.






6.3.3 What Is Left Out


A conductor is in where it lies within what is left out on its layer, otherwise out. Each polygon of the merged markers, and each instance of a cut cell, stands for a model of its own, which is called a block below.







A capacitance partly within a marker is split: for an overlap by its area, for a sidewall or fringe along its edge. A fringe goes by the plate next to the edge, also on a well that goes on across a marker.


The resistance network has no resistance within a block. A via is within a block by its center, on both of its conductors, as vias can stick out past their metal, and the resistance of a part of a via would be made up. Otherwise it keeps its resistance and the metal it lands on.


Devices within a marker stay in the netlist, as the PDK inductors do. In white-box mode (--blackbox n), a capacitor within a marker is lost, as the device is removed and its plates are filtered. A warning names these devices. The devices of a cut cell are left out (Section 6.3.7).


A marker over routing costs that wire much of its capacitance, so a warning names the nets partly within markers, with their layers.






6.3.4 The Variants


Figure 22 shows the three values of --exclusion-markers for a wire through a marker. A --mode CC netlist has one node per net, so tie and ports are the same there, and a warning says that it has no ports for a model.









6.3.4.1 A Wire Through a Marker


Test pattern exclusion_wire_through, a Metal3 wire of 60 µm x 2 µm with a marker over its middle third, is the example of the variants below:


GDS: https://github.com/iic-jku/klayout-pex/blob/main/testdata/designs/ihp-sg13g2/test_patterns/exclusion_wire_through.gds.gz
























6.3.4.2 ignore


What is within a marker is extracted like the rest of the layout. This is the default, as Figure 24 shows:


.SUBCKT exclusion_wire_through A B sub!
Cext_1 A sub! 2.66364f
Cext_2 B sub! 2.66364f
Rext_1 A A|B 0.001
Rext_2 A B 2.596
.ENDS exclusion_wire_through



















6.3.4.3 tie


What is within a marker has no parasitics, and each net stays connected across it, so that the netlist simulates without a model. It’s useful to see what the rest of a layout adds, or if a model is only needed for some of the analyses (Figure 25):


.SUBCKT exclusion_wire_through A B sub!
Cext_1 A sub! 0.951336f
Cext_2 A|B sub! 1.69065f
Cext_3 B sub! 0.951336f
Rext_1 A A|B 0.857956
Rext_2 A|B B 0.858
.ENDS exclusion_wire_through

















6.3.4.3.1 Metal Joined Only Outside the Marker


The metal within a marker stays apart where nothing within the marker joins it. In the test pattern exclusion_stubs (Figure 26), two stubs of a net end within the marker, which only the metal outside it joins. So their pins S1 and S2 stay two nodes, with 1.046 Ω to A each, as a tie would short the metal outside the marker.





















6.3.4.4 ports


Each cut of a net at a marker is a port of the netlist, for a model to connect (Figure 27):


.SUBCKT exclusion_wire_through A A_B__m0_0 A_B__m0_1 B sub!
Cext_1 A sub! 0.951336f
Cext_2 A_B__m0_0 sub! 0.845326f
Cext_3 A_B__m0_1 sub! 0.845326f
Cext_4 B sub! 0.951336f
Rext_1 A A|B 0.001
Rext_2 A A_B__m0_0 0.857956
Rext_3 A_B__m0_1 B 0.858
.ENDS exclusion_wire_through















A port is named after the pin of the net within the marker that is nearest to the cut, on its layer before others, otherwise <net>__m<marker>_<number>. So labels within a marker name the ports. In exclusion_stubs, these are S1 and S2. Such a pin only names a cut of the metal it is joined to within the marker, and not if the net has a pin of that label outside the marker, as a port is one node. A net entirely within a marker has a port at its pin.


--check accepts the pieces of a net that only these ports join. These pieces stay apart in the netlist, also where taps or wells would join them ideally otherwise, as that would short the model. And a part of a well beyond a cut keeps its port and its resistance, with the bulks of the devices on it. A bulk within the marker is a port of the model as well.


A port is one node, which is right across the current, also on a wide wire. Where the metal goes on beside a marker, along a cut, the whole cut would short that metal, so the port is a piece of 1 µm in the middle of the cut. The metal beside it then carries the current alone: test pattern cut_strip_along_wire, a wire of 100 µm x 1 µm with half of its width within a marker along 50 µm, has 8.78 Ω flat and 17.41 Ω with ports, as a port can’t connect a model in parallel to that metal.




6.3.4.4.1 Capacitances Between the Parts of a Net


Metal that only a model joins is one net in LVS, but apart in the netlist with ports, so the capacitances between it count, unlike within a net otherwise. In test pattern exclusion_hairpin (Figure 28), two Metal3 wires 2 µm apart end within the marker, where a bridge joins them. In exclusion_hairpin_open, the bridge has a gap, so they are two nets. With ports, both have the same values:


GDS: https://github.com/iic-jku/klayout-pex/blob/main/testdata/designs/ihp-sg13g2/test_patterns/exclusion_hairpin.gds.gz




















With tie, the net stays connected, so these wires are a net like without a marker, which has no capacitances within it. In --mode CC, a net is one node, so there are no ports and no such capacitances.






6.3.4.4.2 Checking a Model


To check that a model fits, a test extracts the part of the wire within the marker on its own, as a stand-in for a model, connects it between the ports, and compares the port admittance in ngspice with the one of the flat extraction. They differ by 2.3 %, by the fringe of that part at the cuts, where the flat wire has no edges.










6.3.5 Examples




6.3.5.1 A Neighbor Outside a Marker


Test pattern exclusion_plate_neighbor (Figure 29), a Metal3 plate P just within a marker, with a Metal3 wire N 0.3 µm beside it. N keeps all of its values, as it is out, and P keeps only its capacitance to N.


GDS: https://github.com/iic-jku/klayout-pex/blob/main/testdata/designs/ihp-sg13g2/test_patterns/exclusion_plate_neighbor.gds.gz




















Without a label on the plate, in exclusion_floating_plate_neighbor, nothing connects it to the netlist, so that the capacitance to it goes to the substrate: N ↔︎ VSUBS is 5.045 fF.






6.3.5.2 Two Markers


Two such plates P and Q, 0.5 µm apart. With a marker each (exclusion_plates_2_markers), they keep their 0.828 fF to each other, as neither model has it. With one marker over both (exclusion_plates_1_marker), the netlist has no capacitances at all.






6.3.5.3 Vias


Test pattern exclusion_via_stack, a wire from A to B on Metal2, with a bridge on Metal3 over a gap in the middle, with a marker around the bridge:







In exclusion_via_across, the center of the via is outside the marker, so it keeps its 2.031 Ω, and only the Metal3 within the marker has no resistance.






6.3.5.4 Devices


Test pattern exclusion_nmos_diode2 (Figure 30), with a marker over a MOS transistor. The metal of its nets leaves the marker on Metal1 and Metal2.


GDS: https://github.com/iic-jku/klayout-pex/blob/main/testdata/designs/ihp-sg13g2/test_patterns/exclusion_nmos_diode2.gds.gz















With tie, its terminals are on the nodes of the metal within the marker. With ports, each terminal is a port of its own, as the model connects them:


X$1 VSS__m0_2 VDD__m0_4 VDD__m0_5 sub! sg13_lv_nmos w=1.5e-07 l=1.7e-07


The bulk stays on the substrate, which is no conductor of the resistance network.








6.3.6 Markers of a Layer, of a Pair and of the User


--exclusion-marker-layer selects the markers, instead of those on by default. It takes the name of a marker of the PDK, or any GDS layer, for all layers of the stack (200/0) or for some (200/0:met2,met3). So a PDK without markers can have them too, such as sky130A and gf180mcuD, and --exclusion-markers ignore stays the default.


A marker of a layer leaves out only what is on that layer. In test pattern exclusion_plate_noqrc, a Metal3 plate P is between a Metal2 wire A and a Metal4 wire B, with Metal3.noqrc over the plate. So P loses its capacitance to the substrate, and the wires keep all of theirs, with the plate as a shield between them. This is the case that Table 33 is about.


A pair marker only leaves out the capacitances between its two layers, so it has no effect on the resistances. The same plate with m2m3 (exclusion_plate_pair_m2m3), and with m3sub (exclusion_plate_pair_m3sub):







The 0.198 fF that stay with m2m3 are the fringe to the part of A beyond the marker.






6.3.7 Cutting Out a Cell


--cut CELL[=PREFIX] leaves the instances of a cell to a model. CELL is a name or a glob pattern, and a cell within a cut cell is part of it. Each --cut needs instances of its own: the first one that matches a cell takes them.


What is left out:


    

  • The shapes of the cell, on the layers of the stack, so routing over it stays extracted, unlike with a marker over all layers:

      

    • metal and wells by their drawn layers, with the fill that LVS joins to them
      • 

    • what LVS computes from the diffusion (e.g. source and drain) by the diffusion of the cell
      • 

    • not its boundary or the overhang of its wells and implants, which take nothing of the layout under them
      • 

    • 

  • The devices of the cell, also for --check. As the netlist of LVS is flat, they go by what the cell draws at their terminals, on the layers that LVS makes a device of that class from, which the tech info has (the diffusion and the gate of a MOS, the marker of a resistor, a diode, a BJT or a capacitor):

      

    • on each layer, the cell has to draw a polygon at all terminals, and more of them than the rest of the layout, as a diffusion can go on beyond a cell, and a tap can overlap the one of a neighbor
      • 

    • so a device stays if it’s under the boundary or the fill of a cell, beside it on the same diffusion, or has only wires of the cell on its terminals
      • 

    • and fill, a boundary or a wire of the top cell leaves a device to the cell
      • 

    • 

  • Diffusion that no layer draws, which LVS fills up for a device of the cell (e.g. the drain of an LDMOS, across the gap to its gate), but not what the rest of the layout draws
    • 



--cut-keep-net NET takes the shapes of a net out of the cell, also its wells, so that they are extracted like the rest of the layout, e.g. a guard ring.


Where a net enters the cell is a port of the netlist, as with --exclusion-markers ports, named:


    

  • <prefix>__<label>, by the labels of the cell on the metal it is joined to within the cell, nearest first. Several cuts of that metal share the port, as they are one pin of the model
    • 

  • <prefix>__<terminal>, for a terminal of a device of the cell on the metal around it, numbered if the block has several such nodes on a net (X__S_0, X__S_1)
    • 

  • <prefix>__<net>_<number> otherwise
    • 



The prefix:


    

  • is PREFIX for a single instance, with a number for several (x_0, x_1)
    • 

  • is by default the name of the cell with a number per cell (coil_0)
    • 

  • has letters, digits and _ only, as it names ports
    • 

  • has to differ for each instance, so --cut a=S_0 --cut b=S is an error if b has several instances
    • 



Test pattern cut_block_with_mos has the MOS of the design nmos_diode2 in the cell block, whose pins VDD and VSS on Metal3 the top cell wires on to A and B, and a Metal5 wire R over the cell (Figure 31). With --cut block=X:


GDS: https://github.com/iic-jku/klayout-pex/blob/main/testdata/designs/ihp-sg13g2/test_patterns/cut_block_with_mos.gds.gz







.SUBCKT cut_block_with_mos A X__VSS B X__VDD sub! R
Cext_1 A B 0.397445f
Cext_2 A R 0.016564f
Cext_3 A sub! 0.197343f
Cext_4 A X__VDD 0.07352f
Cext_5 B R 0.0584666f
Cext_6 B sub! 0.221065f
Cext_7 R sub! 1.40824f
Cext_8 R X__VDD 0.194269f
Cext_9 R X__VSS 0.0809391f
Cext_10 sub! X__VDD 0.178802f
Cext_11 sub! X__VSS 0.178581f
Cext_12 X__VDD X__VSS 0.4502f
Rext_1 A X__VSS 2.86
Rext_2 B X__VDD 2.86
.ENDS cut_block_with_mos


There is no MOS, the two nets end on the ports for the model, the wire R keeps its capacitances, also to the metal of the cell, and the 2.86 Ω are the ones of the wires of the top cell.






6.3.8 Leaving Out a Net


--exclude-net NET, a name or a glob pattern, is for a net that something else models or drives, such as the power grid of a block:


    

  • it has no resistance, so the netlist has one node for it, which also all of its device terminals are on
    • 

  • it has no capacitance to the substrate
    • 

  • the capacitances between it and other nets stay, as they are the load of those nets, also between two excluded nets, and to a well of another net
    • 



exclusion_plate_neighbor with --exclude-net P gives the values of tie in Table 37, without needing a marker or a GDS. exclusion_nmos_diode2 with --exclude-net 'V*' in --mode RC has no resistor at all, and only 0.492 fF between VDD and VSS.


The values of the nets around it are as without the option, as the net stays in the field model. Unlike with a block, this goes by the name of the net, so that a large grid doesn’t slow down the extraction.






6.3.9 Field Solvers


A field solver only tells the capacitances between its conductors, not where they end on them. So with these options, a net is one conductor for its part outside the blocks, and one for each set of blocks it is within, as these can overlap. The substrate is a conductor of its own, also if its net has metal. There are no panels between the conductors of a net, as those would be coincident. The matrix goes through the rule of Table 34, and the parts of each net are summed up: with all at the same potential, the charges they induce add up to the charge of the net as one conductor.


The netlist of a field solver has one node per net, so it has no ports, as with --mode CC. A warning says so, with ports and with --cut. It also has no capacitances between the parts of a net that only a model joins.


FasterCap gives the same picture as Table 37 and Table 43, with its own values:







Where a net is two conductors, the values around it differ by up to 2.5 %, as the mesh differs at the ends of the parts.






6.3.10 Use Cases




6.3.10.1 Inductor of the PDK, with EM Model


The pcells draw NoRCX.drawing, and the LVS deck of KPEX recognizes the inductor as a subcircuit with its terminals at its leads, so a model replaces it by its name, without any ports. What --exclusion-markers changes is the rest of what is within its polygon, such as a wire under the coil (exclusion_inductor2_wire_under, Figure 32, with --blackbox y):


GDS: https://github.com/iic-jku/klayout-pex/blob/main/testdata/designs/ihp-sg13g2/test_patterns/exclusion_inductor2_wire_under.gds.gz




















So a model of the coil that has that wire in its simulation should be used with tie or ports, and one without with ignore.


This is what #121 asks for: most of a circuit with the 2.5D engine, and EM models for the sensitive RF parts.






6.3.10.2 Coil of LC Oscillator


#213 extracts the core of an oscillator without the coil of its tank, which has an EM-fitted model, but with its leads and its guard ring, with ports where the core meets the coil. Outside KPEX, this took a cut of the GDS, with workarounds for the recognition texts of devices and the labels of child cells.


Test pattern cut_coil (Figure 33) is a small layout with these parts, not that design:


    

  • the cell coil, with a TopMetal2 loop with stubs of its leads, a center tap on TopMetal1, and a TopMetal1 guard ring around them, and the labels LA, LB and CT
    • 

  • wires of the top cell, which go on from the stubs to OSCP, OSCN and VCT, and a stub with the label VDD on the guard ring
    • 

  • a Metal5 wire VC of the top cell under the coil
    • 



GDS: https://github.com/iic-jku/klayout-pex/blob/main/testdata/designs/ihp-sg13g2/test_patterns/cut_coil.gds.gz















With kpex extract --pdk ihp-sg13g2 --gds cut_coil.gds.gz --2.5D --mode RC --cut coil=xind --cut-keep-net VDD:


.SUBCKT cut_coil OSCN OSCP VCT xind__CT xind__LA xind__LB VC VDD sub!
Cext_1 OSCN sub! 1.04552f
Cext_2 OSCP sub! 1.04552f
Cext_3 VC VDD 2.1086f
Cext_4 VC sub! 8.43019f
Cext_5 VC xind__CT 0.89613f
Cext_6 VC xind__LA 0.398954f
Cext_7 VC xind__LB 0.398954f
Cext_8 VCT sub! 1.17194f
Cext_9 VDD sub! 30.0624f
Cext_10 VDD xind__LA 0.110313f
Cext_11 VDD xind__LB 0.110313f
Cext_12 sub! xind__CT 0.925084f
Cext_13 sub! xind__LA 0.703486f
Cext_14 sub! xind__LB 0.703486f
Rext_1 OSCN OSCN|OSCP|VCT 0.001
Rext_2 OSCN xind__LB 0.0348333333333
Rext_3 OSCP xind__LA 0.0348333333333
Rext_4 VCT xind__CT 0.0855
.ENDS cut_coil


The model goes between the ports, in the netlist that includes this one:


XCORE OSCN OSCP VCT xind__CT xind__LA xind__LB VC VDD 0 cut_coil
XL xind__LA xind__LB xind__CT coil_em_model


--mode CC shows what is left out, with the net of the coil being OSCN,OSCP,VCT:







The wire VC, which is no shape of the cell, keeps all of its capacitances, also to the coil, which a model wouldn’t know. Without --cut-keep-net VDD, the guard ring is left to the model too, and the net VDD enters the cell at the port xind__VDD_0.


To check that this fits, a test extracts the coil on its own (cut_coil_model), as a stand-in for a model, connects it between the ports, and compares the port admittance in ngspice with the one of the flat extraction:


    

  • the resistances, between OSCP, OSCN and VCT, are the same within 0.1 %
    • 

  • so are the values of VC and VDD to each other and to the substrate, and their capacitances to the coil in sum, which are at the ports instead of along the coil
    • 

  • the coil to the substrate is 10 % higher, as a model on its own has no shielding by the wires around it
    • 



Compared with the cut of the GDS:


    

  • running LVS on the whole layout keeps the recognition texts of the devices, and needs no selection of the labels of child cells
    • 

  • the ports go by the metal, wherever a net enters, so that the leads need no pins, and the nets their names from the top level
    • 

  • what a block has around it stays in the field model
    • 



--exclusion-markers ports does the same without a cell, for a marker drawn over the coil, inside the guard ring, as in test pattern exclusion_coil_guard_ring (Figure 34), whose labels name the ports. As a marker applies to all layers, routing through it is left out too.




















The second part of #213, every label a port for the wiring between hard blocks, is what the netlists of --mode R and RC do for the labels of a net in the top cell. Labels in the cells of the blocks become ports with --cut.






6.3.10.3 Power Grid of Block


#85 extracts a block whose power grid is part of the top level:


kpex extract --pdk ihp-sg13g2 --gds block.gds.gz --2.5D --mode RC \
             --exclude-net VDD --exclude-net VSS


So VDD and VSS are ideal nodes of the netlist, with all device terminals on them, and each signal keeps its load to them, as the grid stays in the field model. For debugging, leaving out the resistance of one net at a time shows what it adds to a simulation.








6.3.11 Limits


    

  • A model whose simulation includes a neighbor counts their coupling twice, unless the neighbor is within the block too. The boundary of such hybrid flows seems to be little studied: the literature has the error of ports within an EM model (Rautio 2008), but no work on the double counting was found
    • 

  • A model extracted or simulated on its own has no shielding by what is around it (Section 6.3.10)
    • 

  • The coupling of a conductor outside to one within a block lands on the nearest node of its net, which is approximate in a large block
    • 

  • KLayout’s square counting, which the resistance network uses, has the current along the longest edge of each convex part of a polygon, also without these options. So a part beyond a cut that is shorter than it is wide has too little resistance, which matters on wells: two nwell taps of r_ntap_pair_nwell_li1_m1, with a marker of 2 µm between them across the nwell of 7 µm, have 212 Ω with tie, 1948 Ω by tessellation. Wires at an angle have too little too, a Metal3 wire of 60 µm x 1 µm has 5.28 Ω at 0° and 2.65 Ω at 45°, and a corner of a marker on such a wire can give several times the value of the whole wire
    • 

  • A net that goes on from one cut cell to another, where they abut, has no port between them, for which a warning names the net and the cells
    • 

  • --cut of an instance at an angle other than a multiple of 90°, or of one with such an instance below it, is an error, as the LVS database only has the bounding boxes of the shapes of such an instance
    • 

  • There is no comparison with silicon or an EM simulation yet: the reference of tie, ports and --cut is the flat extraction
    • 

  • The exports of 2.5D scenes for other field solvers don’t honor these options. MAGIC doesn’t either, so they are an error together with it
    • 









6.4 Connecting the Extracted Netlist


A parasitic netlist has two jobs: describe the layout’s electrical network, and expose an interface that the testbench can call correctly. A correct capacitance attached to the wrong positional pin is still a wrong simulation.


--schematic supplies two pieces of that interface to KPEX/2.5D: the order of the top-level ports, and names for devices that can be matched unambiguously. It does not replace a full LVS comparison. The checks in Section 8 answer narrower questions about missing devices, geometry totals, pins and connectivity.




6.4.1 Choosing Which Labels Become Ports


A label inside a child cell often names an internal net. Making every such label a top-level port can expose implementation details of a block to its testbench. Conversely, a layout without top-level pin labels may rely on the labels of its children.







auto is the default. --port-labels top needs --gds, including when an LVS database supplies the extracted nets. Substrate handling and top-level text-only ports remain in place. Selecting top-level labels does not remove the child geometry or the internal nets from extraction.






6.4.2 Keeping Positional Calls Correct


SPICE connects a subcircuit call by position. The first node in the call connects to the first port of its .subckt declaration, regardless of the spelling of the two names.


KPEX/2.5D defines the exported order as follows:


    

  • With --schematic, the matching top subcircuit’s ports come first, in schematic order
    • 

  • Any remaining ports follow, sorted by name, comparing without case first and exact spelling second
    • 

  • Without a usable schematic top, all exported ports use that name order
    • 

  • Matching ignores case, while the exported spelling comes from the extracted net
    • 



This applies to CC, C, R and RC, to reduced netlists, to SPICE and VACASK, and to the port lists recorded in kpex_result.json. It changes the interface order, not which physical net each port connects to. In CC and C, several labels on one equipotential net can remain one exported port; its earliest schematic alias determines its position.




6.4.2.1 Transistor with Schematic Port Order


Download ordered.spice, whose top declaration is .subckt nfet_li1 S G D and whose transistor is named Xtail. From the KPEX source directory, run:


kpex extract --pdk sky130A --2.5D --mode CC --blackbox y \
  --gds testdata/designs/sky130A/test_patterns/nfet_li1.gds.gz \
  --schematic ordered.spice --out-netlist ordered-extracted.spice


GDS: https://github.com/iic-jku/klayout-pex/blob/main/testdata/designs/sky130A/test_patterns/nfet_li1.gds.gz


The declaration and device lines from that run are:


.SUBCKT nfet_li1 S G D sky130_gnd
Xtail D G S sky130_gnd sky130_fd_pr__nfet_01v8 l=0.15 w=0.65 as=0.169 ad=0.169
+ ps=1.82 pd=1.82















The top-level interface starts with S G D. The substrate sky130_gnd, absent from the schematic’s port declaration, follows them. The transistor line has its own model terminal order; it need not have the same order as the top-level interface. For this symmetric MOS device, exchanging source and drain still permits the match.








6.4.3 Following Schematic Device Names


Device naming needs a schematic .subckt whose name matches the layout top cell. Port ordering can additionally use the sole uncalled subcircuit when the top name differs; that fallback does not rename devices.


Matching uses the device mappings of the technology, connectivity and device geometry. A successful match retains the schematic name, as Xtail above. Devices inside schematic subcircuits can retain hierarchical paths such as X1.Xtail. Parallel layout fingers of one schematic MOS receive suffixes such as _0, _1 and _2.


Names alone are not evidence that two devices correspond. Indistinguishable parallel schematic instances, missing model mappings or an ambiguous comparison keep layout-derived names and produce a warning. An assignment that would create duplicate output names is rejected. The model mapping still selects the proper SPICE designator, so a native schematic M may be emitted through an X wrapper when that is the PDK’s model interface.






6.4.4 Keeping Geometry Units Separate from Electrical Values


The SPICE directives .option scale=1u and .options scale=1u set one geometry scale for the whole parsed netlist. They are not per-device or per-model settings. A declaration inside a subcircuit still supplies that same global setting.


For scale \(s\), the schematic geometry evaluator applies:







An X parameter named w is not automatically a length: its meaning belongs to the wrapper. If the wrapper is defined in the input, its native devices receive scaling after parameter evaluation. For an external model wrapper, the technology’s device mapping translates its declared units into the layout units used for matching and checks.


This distinction avoids scaling twice. The technology mapping describes the model interface; .options scale describes the netlist’s global geometry convention. Neither should be inferred from the other. Diode area factors and other model-specific parameters also cannot be treated as physical areas just because of their names.


The schematic reader accepts only scale on .option or .options. Keep simulator analyses, .model, .include, .lib and unrelated options in the testbench or model library, outside this input. It is a circuit description reader, not a complete simulation-deck reader.


The parser accepts a finite positive SPICE number, including suffixes. 1u and 1000n express the same scale. SPICE suffixes are case-insensitive: M means milli, and MEG means mega. Identical repeated declarations are accepted, while conflicting values, zero and negative scales are rejected.


The extraction argument --scale y is a different setting: it normalizes the fringe model at the halo boundary (Section 6.2). It does not rescale layout coordinates or SPICE device geometry.






6.4.5 Including Both Files in a VACASK Testbench


Conversion preserves the global setting in a companion options fragment. Download geometry-scale.spice, which contains a native Mnative and an external Xwrapped in parallel, both with w=4 l=2, under .option scale=1u:


netlist convert geometry-scale.spice --to vacask \
  --out-netlist geometry-scale.inc


The circuit include contains:


subckt pair (d g s b)
  Mnative (d g s b) nmos w=4 l=2 ad=3 as=5 pd=7 ps=11
  Xwrapped (d g s b) external w=4 l=2 ad=3 as=5 pd=7 ps=11
ends















The companion geometry-scale.options.inc contains:


options scale=1e-06


Include the circuit at circuit scope, and the options inside the testbench’s existing control block, before analyses:


Geometry scale example

include "geometry-scale-models.inc"
include "geometry-scale.inc"
xpair (d g 0 0) pair
model supply vsource
vd (d 0) supply dc=1 mag=1
vg (g 0) supply dc=1

control
  include "geometry-scale.options.inc"
  analysis op1 op
  analysis ac1 ac values=[1e6]
endc


Save the complete testbench beside the converted files and run vacask geometry-scale.sim. Its operating-point and AC analyses both run with the fragment above.


The example model file defines external as a wrapper around the same native model. The native device therefore sees a width of 4 µm and length of 2 µm in both paths. The X arguments remain unchanged so that the wrapper passes them on in its expected units.


The options affect the whole simulation, including other included circuits and external wrappers. Combining circuits that assume different global scales requires normalizing their model interfaces first. Omitting the options file or applying a second scale to the instance values changes the geometry.


kpex extract --netlist-format vacask --out-netlist extracted.inc also writes a companion extracted.options.inc. Keep both files together, even when the options set scale=1. A converter does not translate model libraries: the testbench must supply compatible VACASK models. With PDK wrappers, pass --pdk to netlist convert so that multiplier handling follows their declared interfaces.


The examples were verified with klayout-pex 0.9.0 and KLayout 0.30.13. The port-order and naming guarantees are independent of the capacitance coefficients that may change in subsequent releases.










7 Choosing Capacitance Coupling


Two neighboring conductors exchange current when their voltages change differently. Keeping that coupling is necessary for crosstalk and charge sharing. A grounded approximation instead describes the load of each conductor when the others are held at the reference potential.












Note







These options belong to the development version following 0.9.0. The released 0.9.0 command line does not yet provide --mode C, --coupling or netlist ground.








7.1 Choosing the Extraction Mode


The analytical engine keeps coupling by default. Select grounded output explicitly:







--mode CC --coupling grounded is equivalent to --mode C. --coupling coupled explicitly retains the default policy for CC or RC. It cannot be combined with C. R has no capacitance policy to select.


For grounded capacitance with ideal interconnects:


kpex extract --pdk sky130A --2.5D --mode C --blackbox y \
  --gds layout.gds --out-netlist layout-c.spice


For grounded coupling while retaining the distributed resistance:


kpex extract --pdk sky130A --2.5D --mode RC \
  --coupling grounded --blackbox y \
  --gds layout.gds --out-netlist layout-rc.spice


The reference is the extracted substrate net, or VSUBS when no substrate net is available. It is not implicitly SPICE node 0. Connect the exported reference to the intended testbench potential.






7.2 Eliminating Floating Conductors First


A floating conductor has no port or retained device terminal that can drive it. It can still transfer charge between other conductors. Connecting it to the reference would change that transfer, so floating capacitance is eliminated before any coupling is grounded.


Consider A ↔︎ F with 3 pF and F ↔︎ B with 6 pF, where F is floating. The two capacitors form a series connection:


\[
C_{AB}=\frac{C_{AF}C_{FB}}{C_{AF}+C_{FB}}
       =\frac{3\times6}{3+6}\;\mathrm{pF}=2\;\mathrm{pF}.
\]


The first transformation is exact for this capacitor network. The subsequent replacement of A ↔︎ B by loads to the reference is an approximation.











7.2.1 Reproducing the Floating Example


Download floating-divider.spice:


.subckt divider A B VSS
Cext_af A F 3p
Cext_fb F B 6p
.ends divider


Run:


netlist ground floating-divider.spice --reference VSS \
  --out-netlist grounded-divider.spice


The written output contains:


.subckt divider A B VSS
* netlist ground: exact floating elimination, then full inter-net loads to VSS
Cgrnd_1 A VSS 2p
Cgrnd_2 B VSS 2p
.ends divider


No element ties F to VSS. The node disappears through elimination. Grounding F first would have produced unequal 3 pF and 6 pF loads instead of the two 2 pF loads above.






7.2.2 Extending the Elimination to a Network


For a floating node connected to several neighbors, eliminating its voltage adds a capacitance between every pair of neighbors:


\[
C_{ij}^{\mathrm{added}}=
\frac{C_{iF}C_{Fj}}{\sum_k C_{Fk}}.
\]


Existing parallel capacitances add to these contributions. Repeating the operation gives the Schur complement of the floating block of the capacitance matrix:


\[
\mathbf C_{\mathrm{retained}}=
\mathbf C_{tt}-\mathbf C_{tf}\mathbf C_{ff}^{-1}\mathbf C_{ft}.
\]


The expression explains the result. The calculation uses sparse node elimination. An isolated component with no observable connection contributes no terminal load. A floating component attached to only one retained node also contributes no load: its potential follows that node.


Ports created by labels and exclusion interfaces remain observable. The log names eliminated floating conductors, so an unintentionally disconnected supply can be distinguished from intended floating fill.








7.3 Replacing Coupling by Grounded Loads


After floating elimination, a capacitance \(C\) between distinct retained conductors becomes \(C\) to the reference at each endpoint. It is not divided in half.


For a single pair, with voltages measured relative to the reference:


\[
\begin{bmatrix}i_A\\i_B\end{bmatrix}
=j\omega
\begin{bmatrix}C&-C\\-C&C\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}v_A\\v_B\end{bmatrix}
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
j\omega
\begin{bmatrix}C&0\\0&C\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}v_A\\v_B\end{bmatrix}.
\]


This preserves the diagonal of the reduced nodal capacitance matrix after floating elimination. It removes transfer admittance between conductors. With distributed resistance, capacitance between nodes of the same conductor remains at its original endpoints.


This is a nodal capacitance property, not a general equality of RC port admittance. Holding an external port at the reference does not clamp every internal node behind its wire resistance.


For the ideal-conductor pair above, the approximation has a specific operating assumption:







Grounded output therefore does not provide a universal worst case. Use coupled output to study crosstalk, differential switching or charge sharing. No switching multiplier or capacitance threshold is inferred.






7.4 Grounding an Existing Netlist


netlist ground performs the same transformation without loading a layout or PDK. It selects parasitic elements and one SPICE scope, retains the rest of the input, and writes a separate file.




7.4.1 Distributed Wires and Intentional Capacitance


Download coupled-rc.spice. A1 belongs to conductor A through Rext_a. B1 belongs to B through Rext_b. F is capacitor-only floating fill. Cload is an intentional capacitor that is outside the default parasitic selection.


.subckt coupled A B VSS
Rext_a A A1 100
Rext_b B B1 200
Cext_ab A1 B1 2p
Cext_af A1 F 3p
Cext_fb F B1 6p
Cext_sub A1 VSS 1p
Cload A VSS 5p
.ends coupled




Run:


netlist ground coupled-rc.spice --reference VSS \
  --out-netlist grounded-rc.spice


Eliminating F adds 2 pF to the existing 2 pF coupling. The resulting 4 pF is grounded at A1 and B1. A1 already has 1 pF to VSS, giving 5 pF there. The written output is:


.subckt coupled A B VSS
Rext_a A A1 100
Rext_b B B1 200
* netlist ground: exact floating elimination, then full inter-net loads to VSS
Cgrnd_1 A1 VSS 5p
Cgrnd_2 B1 VSS 4p
Cload A VSS 5p
.ends coupled







The two resistor lines and Cload remain unchanged. The grounded loads stay behind the wire resistances. They are not moved to ports A and B. Existing capacitance to a distributed reference node also stays on that node, preserving its reference-side resistance.






7.4.2 Selecting Parasitics and the Reference







Names and patterns are case-insensitive. Capacitor patterns must start with C and resistor patterns with R, so a bare * is rejected. Quote patterns so the shell does not expand them. For a different extractor’s naming convention:


netlist ground extracted.spice --cell amplifier --reference VSS \
  --capacitor 'Cpar_*' --resistor 'Rwire_*' --keep bias_internal


Subcircuit ports, globals, terminals on retained device/source lines and --keep nodes retain their conductors. A capacitance does not make a DC connection between conductors. Selected resistors do, but their finite values and textual representation remain in the output.


The reference is local to the selected scope. SPICE ground aliases 0 and gnd identify the same reference conductor for this transformation. Unrelated names such as VSS do not become ground implicitly.






7.4.3 Identifying Disconnected Pieces of One Conductor


A netlist alone may not reveal that two disconnected wire pieces belong to one original layout net. Supply that identity explicitly in a flat JSON object:


{"OUT.1": "OUT", "OUT.2": "OUT"}


Save it as nodes.json and add --net-map nodes.json. The map groups conductor identities for the coupling decision. It does not short the nodes, rename them or add a resistor. It cannot assign different conductors to nodes already joined by selected resistors.








7.5 Keeping the Approximation Separate from Other Checks


Grounding occurs after capacitance has been assigned to distributed nodes and before optional network reduction. A reduction check therefore compares the grounded network with its further reduced version. It does not certify equivalence to the original coupled network.


The geometry reports and --check-device-caps continue to describe the coupled extraction. Intentional capacitor models remain in place with --blackbox y. When a layout contains metal capacitors that white-box extraction would remove, grounded output asks for --blackbox y before capacitance extraction. Once device capacitance and parasitics have been mixed in a plain netlist, postprocessing cannot recover that distinction.






7.6 Limits


    

  • RC grounding rejects floating islands containing resistance because their frequency-dependent response cannot generally be replaced by fixed capacitors
    • 

  • C uses ideal conductors and can eliminate their floating capacitance network exactly
    • 

  • Exact elimination stops if a remaining floating node exceeds the 64-neighbor fill-in limit after other floating nodes have been removed
    • 

  • Standalone selection requires numeric two-node resistor and capacitor primitives
    • 

  • Selected resistor values must be strictly positive
    • 

  • Symbolic values and ambiguous scopes produce diagnostics
    • 

  • netlist ground refuses to overwrite its input and validates the selection before writing output
    • 

  • The extraction options apply only to --2.5D
    • 



Keep coupled output for unsupported floating networks. Grounded output does not tie a remaining floating island to the reference as a fallback.








8 Checking Extracted Netlists


A plausible simulation result does not establish that an extracted netlist is complete. A device terminal can be disconnected from the resistance of its wire, a port can be missing, or a reduction can remove the loss that matters at the operating frequency. These failures need different comparisons.


KPEX/2.5D checks the following stages:







The structural checks guard the translation from layout connectivity into a netlist. The admittance check guards a subsequent approximation. The device comparison examines the physical capacitance estimate itself. Passing one does not imply that the other two pass.




8.1 Preserving Layout Connectivity


Resistance extraction splits one layout net into many nodes. These node names need not resemble the original net name, and device names may come from the schematic (Section 6.4.3). The structural comparison therefore follows the layout’s net identities and device identities, rather than trying to infer connectivity from spelling.


For each original net, KPEX follows the connected component formed by its parasitic resistors. Capacitors do not join these components: they couple nets electrically, but do not make a DC connection.


The comparison looks for:


    

  • Original nets missing from the expanded netlist
    • 

  • Resistors that incorrectly join two original nets
    • 

  • Resistor components that reach no original net or model interface port
    • 

  • Device terminals attached to the wrong net’s resistor network
    • 

  • Device terminals attached to a different node than their extracted terminal port
    • 

  • Missing device instances, or retained whiteboxed devices that would count their capacitance twice
    • 

  • Missing ports and ports that touch nothing, with the exceptions required by exclusion interfaces
    • 

  • Node names that collide when SPICE treats names without regard to case
    • 



For capacitance, the comparison first maps the distributed nodes back to their original nets. It then sums the parasitic capacitors for every pair of nets, and compares these sums with the extraction summary. The relative tolerance is \(10^{-9}\); this comparison allows rounding, not a physical modeling error. A capacitance to the substrate is omitted from this comparison if the chosen substrate connection shorts its two endpoints together.




8.1.1 Choosing Whether a Structural Problem Stops the Run


In --mode RC, structural problems fail the run by default. In the other modes they are warnings by default. --check y makes them failures explicitly, and --check n accepts the netlist while keeping the warnings visible.


The checks run on the full extracted network before reduction. A reduction therefore cannot hide a structural defect by removing the affected nodes. For a structural failure found after extraction, the netlist remains available for inspection.


A separate warning identifies nets with parasitic elements but no device terminal or port that can drive them. Floating fill can legitimately produce this warning. A supply rail under a wrong label can produce it too, so it deserves review. This warning alone does not fail --check.








8.2 Comparing with the Schematic


With --schematic, KPEX also compares the extracted devices with the schematic, using the technology’s device mappings (Section 3.6). These checks supplement LVS; they do not perform a complete schematic-versus-layout topology comparison.




8.2.1 Comparing Device Quantities


Counting instances is insufficient. One schematic MOS instance can become several parallel fingers in the layout. Conversely, a layout extractor can combine devices. The comparison uses totals that survive these representations:


    

  • Device-class presence
    • 

  • Total \(W L\) when both dimensions are mapped, or total area when an area is mapped instead
    • 

  • Total \(W\) for mapped MOS devices
    • 

  • Total mapped multiplicity, such as emitter count
    • 



Multipliers and the number of hierarchical instances are included. Schematic dimensions are converted back to the LVS units before summation, including the SPICE geometry scaling discussed in Section 6.4.4. The relative tolerance for device totals is \(10^{-6}\).


A missing parameter is not silently replaced by an invented value. If the schematic leaves a relevant quantity to a model default, the corresponding total is left out and reported. A class without mapped totals is checked for presence only. Equal totals can still conceal an incorrectly wired device, which is why they do not replace LVS.






8.2.2 Comparing Pins and Ports


The top schematic subcircuit is selected by the layout cell name, without regard to case. If that name is absent, the schematic must have exactly one subcircuit that no other element calls.


The comparison reports schematic pins without extracted ports, and extracted ports without schematic pins. It accounts for interfaces that extraction adds or treats specially:


    

  • The selected substrate net may be global in the schematic
    • 

  • Exclusion-marker and cut-cell model ports are extra interfaces
    • 

  • A schematic pin that reaches only mapped bulk terminals can be absent from the extracted ports
    • 

  • A bulk-only pin is compared normally if an extracted port has its name
    • 



Port order is a separate interface contract, described in Section 6.4.2.








8.3 Checking the Response after Reduction


A smaller netlist should present nearly the same electrical response to its surroundings. Rather than comparing resistor counts or individual component values, the admittance check asks:




For the same terminal voltages at this frequency, how much do the resulting terminal currents change?




The check is optional because exact elimination can be more expensive than the reduction itself. It works with netlist reduce, and with kpex extract --2.5D --reduce floating or --reduce ticer in R or RC mode.




8.3.1 From Branches to Terminal Admittance


At frequency \(f\), a branch with conductance \(g\) and capacitance \(c\) has complex admittance


\[
y(f)=g+j\omega c, \qquad \omega=2\pi f.
\]


A branch between nodes \(a\) and \(b\) adds \(+y\) to both diagonal entries of the nodal admittance matrix, and \(-y\) to the two off-diagonal entries. This gives


\[
\mathbf i = \mathbf Y(f)\,\mathbf v,
\qquad \mathbf Y(f)=\mathbf G+j\omega\mathbf C.
\]


Partition the nodes into terminals \(t\) that the surrounding circuit can observe, and internal nodes \(i\) that it cannot drive directly:


\[
\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf i_t\\\mathbf 0\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf Y_{tt}&\mathbf Y_{ti}\\
\mathbf Y_{it}&\mathbf Y_{ii}
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf v_t\\\mathbf v_i\end{bmatrix}.
\]


Eliminating the internal voltages gives the terminal response


\[
\mathbf Y_{\mathrm{term}}
=\mathbf Y_{tt}-\mathbf Y_{ti}\mathbf Y_{ii}^{-1}\mathbf Y_{it}.
\]


This is a Schur complement. The implementation performs sparse, complex node elimination rather than forming a dense inverse. For one internal star node, eliminating it adds a branch between each pair of its neighbors:


\[
y_{ab}^{\mathrm{added}}=
\frac{y_{an}y_{nb}}{\sum_k y_{nk}}.
\]


This evaluation uses the full complex admittances at the requested frequency. It is independent of the approximate low-frequency reduction described in Section 10.


The terminals include the subcircuit ports, global and ground nodes, nodes touched by non-plain-R/C lines, and nodes selected with netlist reduce --keep. In particular, device and subcircuit terminals remain observable. The global reference 0 is also included so that added tie resistors affect the comparison.


Each subcircuit and the top level are evaluated separately. Components with no path to an observed terminal at that frequency do not contribute. At DC, capacitors are open circuits. The check does not add artificial ground conductances to make an isolated component solvable.






8.3.2 Comparing the Two Matrices


The reported error is


\[
\varepsilon(f)=
\frac{\left\|\mathbf Y_{\mathrm{reduced}}(f)
                 -\mathbf Y_{\mathrm{original}}(f)\right\|_F}
     {\left\|\mathbf Y_{\mathrm{original}}(f)\right\|_F},
\qquad
\|\mathbf Y\|_F=\sqrt{\sum_{a,b}|Y_{ab}|^2}.
\]


Both real and imaginary parts contribute. The check reads the written netlists, so its result includes rounded component values and any real tie resistors introduced by reduction.


The default limit is --check-max-relative-error 0.01, or 1%. Equality with the limit passes. The limit must be strictly between zero and one.


There is no absolute-error floor. A tiny capacitance is still compared relatively. Two zero matrices have zero error, while a nonzero reduced response against a zero original response has infinite error.






8.3.3 Choosing Frequencies


Use a single frequency when one operating point is the question. Use a range when the circuit must behave across a band:


netlist reduce extracted.spice \
  --check-frequency-range 1Meg 10G \
  --check-points-per-decade 10 \
  --check-include-dc


--check-frequency-range takes two arguments, the start and stop frequencies. SPICE suffixes are accepted. The endpoints are included, and the samples are logarithmically spaced. The default density is ten points per decade. A partial final decade still includes the exact upper endpoint.


The range requires \(0<f_{\mathrm{start}}\le f_{\mathrm{stop}}\). Equal endpoints produce one positive-frequency sample. --check-include-dc adds a separate sample at zero. For a DC-only check, use --check-frequency 0 instead.


Every sample in every checked scope must pass. The report names the worst sampled error and its frequency. A passing sweep covers those samples, not every frequency between them. Increase the density near an important transition or inspect a simulator response when that distinction matters.






8.3.4 Example: Losing the Series Resistance of a Capacitor


Download the original series-rc.spice. The internal node n has a time constant \(\tau=RC=100\,\mathrm{ps}\). Choosing a threshold of 1n allows its elimination:


netlist reduce series-rc.spice --ticer-tau 1n \
  --check-frequency-range 1Meg 1G \
  --check-points-per-decade 2 --check-include-dc \
  --out-netlist series-rc-reduced.spice


The input contains:


.SUBCKT series_rc A B
R1 A n 100
C1 n B 1p
.ENDS series_rc


The written reduced netlist contains:


.SUBCKT series_rc A B
Cred_1 A B 1p
.ENDS series_rc







For this circuit the original and reduced branch admittances are


\[
y_{\mathrm{original}}=\frac{j\omega C}{1+j\omega RC},
\qquad y_{\mathrm{reduced}}=j\omega C.
\]


Their two-terminal matrices have the same sign pattern, so the Frobenius error reduces to the scalar relative error:


\[
\varepsilon(f)=
\frac{|y_{\mathrm{reduced}}-y_{\mathrm{original}}|}
     {|y_{\mathrm{original}}|}
=\omega RC \quad (f>0).
\]


The run checks eight points, including DC, and exits with code 1. Its reported worst relative Frobenius error is 0.628319 at 1G Hz, against the 0.01 limit. At 1Meg Hz alone it would pass, with relative error 0.000628319.















A smaller threshold preserves the internal node in this example:


netlist reduce series-rc.spice --ticer-tau 1p \
  --check-frequency-range 1Meg 1G \
  --check-points-per-decade 2 --check-include-dc \
  --out-netlist series-rc-kept.spice


This run exits with code 0 and reports zero error at every sampled frequency. It keeps one resistor, one capacitor and three nodes. In a larger network, reducing the threshold usually trades fewer eliminated nodes for a closer response.






8.3.5 Limits of the Admittance Check


The matrix comparison covers the plain, numerically valued resistors and capacitors that the reduction reads. It does not simulate nonlinear device models, resolve a transistor’s bias point, or establish that the extracted parasitic values match silicon.


A relative norm over the whole matrix is not a separate relative bound on every small matrix entry. Nor does a small admittance error guarantee an acceptable quality factor: a small dissipative part can matter even when the much larger capacitive response dominates the norm. Keep the full network or use a sufficiently small reduction threshold when loss is important, and inspect the relevant circuit response.


Exact elimination can create many new couplings. The check limits each evaluation to 100,000 nodes/coupling entries and 1,000,000 coupling updates. It also limits the complete request to 1,001 frequency points and 10,000,000 graph entries/coupling updates across all scopes and samples. Exceeding a limit, or encountering an unevaluable numerical result, fails the requested check rather than silently accepting an unchecked network.








8.4 Comparing Device Capacitance with a Model


A blackboxed capacitor keeps its device model in the netlist. KPEX suppresses coupling between its internal plates so that the netlist does not count that capacitance twice. Ordinarily, that suppression also hides a useful diagnostic: how closely would the geometry-based extraction agree with the device’s nominal capacitance?


--check-device-caps observes those otherwise suppressed contributions. It does not add them to the exported netlist. The prerequisites are --gds, --2.5D, --blackbox y, and --mode CC or --mode RC.




8.4.1 Selecting the Geometry


The comparison identifies the selected device’s recognition marker in the original layout, using its terminal geometry and the recognition layers declared by the technology. It then observes coupling only when both participating plate shapes:


    

  • Belong to that same marker
    • 

  • Belong to the selected pair of terminal nets
    • 

  • Lie wholly inside the marker
    • 



The plate polygons are tagged, rather than clipped. Clipping at the marker boundary would manufacture new edges and therefore change sidewall and fringe contributions. A plate crossing that boundary is reported as unevaluable instead.


The comparison accumulates overlap, sidewall and fringe contributions separately:


\[
C_{\mathrm{geometry}}=
C_{\mathrm{overlap}}+C_{\mathrm{sidewall}}+C_{\mathrm{fringe}},
\qquad
r=\frac{C_{\mathrm{geometry}}}{C_{\mathrm{reference}}}.
\]


This is a device-local measurement. Substrate capacitance, coupling to external routing, and other capacitors connected between the same two net names are not a substitute for it. Output exclusions do not turn it into a subtraction of two whole-net capacitance totals.


Ambiguous geometry is not guessed. Missing or overlapping recognition markers, a marker containing another device’s terminals, shorted selected terminals, and missing internal plate geometry are reported as errors or unevaluable comparisons.






8.4.2 Using the Selected Technology Reference


With no filename after --check-device-caps, the reference comes from the technology’s device mapping (Section 3.6.1). The selected device-reference component supplies an expression, its valid parameter domain, a source and its assumptions. It is evaluated using the mapped device parameters. A nonnominal scenario must explicitly select a matching reference component; Section 3.9.12 describes the supported MIM combinations. The default nominal comparison remains unchanged.


KPEX does not search simulator model libraries at runtime or use an arbitrary LVS capacitance placeholder as the reference. Unsupported metal capacitors are listed as unchecked. If the layout has no available references, the requested comparison fails with an explanation.


There are no default ratio bounds. An evaluable automatic comparison is informational, not a declaration that the extraction is accurate enough for a circuit. This matters especially when the nominal model is itself an engineering estimate.






8.4.3 Example: MOM Plates below a Separate Route


GDS: https://github.com/iic-jku/klayout-pex/blob/v0.9.0/testdata/designs/ihp-sg13g2/test_patterns/cap_cmomf_w10u_l25u_m2_m4_m5_wire.gds.gz















The ihp-sg13g2 example has a cap_cmomf device with Metal2–Metal4 plates, width \(10\,\mu\mathrm m\) and length \(25\,\mu\mathrm m\). A separate Metal5 route on net X crosses above it. The model reference is the nominal mutual capacitance of mim_top ↔︎ mim_btm, with no corner or mismatch variation.


Set KPEX_DIR to the source checkout. This command uses its committed LVS database as well as the GDS, so that the comparison can find the original recognition marker. Here --scale y normalizes the fringe response at the halo, independently of SPICE geometry scaling:


pattern=cap_cmomf_w10u_l25u_m2_m4_m5_wire
layouts="$KPEX_DIR/testdata/designs/ihp-sg13g2/test_patterns"
lvsdbs="$KPEX_DIR/testdata/lvsdb/ihp-sg13g2/test_patterns"
kpex extract --pdk ihp-sg13g2 --2.5D --mode CC \
  --blackbox y --halo 8 --scale y \
  --gds "$layouts/$pattern.gds.gz" \
  --lvsdb "$lvsdbs/$pattern.lvsdb.gz" \
  --check-device-caps --out-dir checks-mom \
  --out-result checks-mom.json


With klayout-pex 0.9.0, including the sidewall counting correction and refreshed nominal coefficients, the comparison reports:


$1 (cap_cmomf), mim_top / mim_btm:
marker coupling 236.403 fF, model reference 228.75 fF,
ratio 1.03345 (informational)


The device comparison is kept separately from the parasitic netlist. The netlist retains the compact-model instance and the external couplings, including those to X and the substrate. checks-mom.json records the comparison in device_capacitance_checks, including the three contributions in farads, the ratio, the reference source and its assumptions.






8.4.4 Supplying References and Acceptance Bounds


An explicit JSON file replaces the automatic selection. It can select one device and terminal pair, supply an independent reference, and optionally make the comparison a pass/fail check. For the preceding example, this reference file specifies an illustrative ±5% acceptance interval:


{
  "format_version": 1,
  "references": [
    {
      "device": "$1",
      "device_class": "cap_cmomf",
      "terminals": ["mim_top", "mim_btm"],
      "capacitance": "228.75f",
      "min_ratio": 0.95,
      "max_ratio": 1.05
    }
  ]
}


Repeat the example command with --check-device-caps mom-reference.json. These bounds pass for the recorded ratio 1.03345, producing exit code 0.




8.4.4.1 Rejected Comparison
